## [RAQ-MLA: Role-Aware Quantization for Multi-Head Latent Attention Caches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33625) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RAQ-MLA proposes a training-free quantization scheme that treats the two tensors cached by Multi-Head Latent Attention differently: the compressed KV latent is optimized against attention-weighted value error, while the narrow positional key is optimized against attention score perturbation. It quantizes the full MLA cache to about 2.5 bits per element, a 6.5x theoretical increase in KV-cache capacity, while remaining nearly lossless on reasoning and coding tasks across four MLA models. Existing KV-cache quantization methods are designed for standard attention's per-head keys and values and ignore MLA's distinct cache structure, leaving accuracy on the table at low bit widths. RAQ-MLA's role-aware analysis closes this gap for frontier models that adopt MLA, enabling longer contexts and higher throughput in memory-bound LLM inference. The method fits an invertible transform to each cached tensor without any training, targeting the specific error that tensor delivers to the attention output rather than generic reconstruction error. The reported 2.5-bit-per-element result and 6.5x capacity gain are theoretical, and the evaluation covers four MLA models on reasoning and coding benchmarks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek-V2, reduces the KV-cache bottleneck by caching a compressed low-rank KV latent instead of per-head keys and values; at decode time this latent is up-projected into keys and values, and a separate narrow positional key carries position information into the attention score. KV-cache quantization stores cached tensors at low bit widths (e.g., FP8 or 4-bit) to fit more tokens in memory and support longer contexts. Prior quantization work assumes the standard key/value cache layout and does not account for MLA's compressed latent plus positional key structure.

## [Power-of-Two Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Neurons Enable Energy-Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33658) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce the Power-of-Two Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (PoT-LIF) neuron, which emits signed spikes with power-of-two amplitudes and uses residual-preserving membrane dynamics to represent continuous information through discrete spikes. Integrated into the vision, vision-language, and action projections of the π0.5 VLA model, PoT-LIF achieves 96.90% success on LIBERO closed-loop episodes at T=1, using approximately 1/7.67 of the dense-reference arithmetic energy (an 86.95% modeled reduction). This work shows that spiking computation can be added to pretrained VLA policies without restructuring them or changing their external inference interfaces, addressing a key barrier to energy-efficient robotic deployment. It could enable VLA models to run on energy-constrained or neuromorphic hardware while preserving closed-loop control performance. The Heartbeat formulation localizes spiking within weighted projections, and the method is evaluated over 2,000 paired closed-loop LIBERO episodes per configuration; Heartbeat mode reaches 97.25% at T=2 and 96.90% at T=4, compared with 96.70% for the continuous-activation π0.5 baseline. The reported 86.95% energy reduction is a modeled arithmetic estimate at T=1 with a 60.01% firing rate, not a measured hardware result.

## [SWE-Ladder: Stage-Specific Self-Distillation for Software Engineering Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33667) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SWE-Ladder introduces a progressive privileged self-distillation method that provides stage-specific supervision for localization, reproduction, and patching of repository-level issues, combined with GRPO for full-trajectory optimization. On SWE-bench Verified with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, it improves pass@1 from 9.6% to 16.4% under the R2E-Gym scaffold and from 13.0% to 17.6% under OpenHands, outperforming GRPO (10.4%) and OPSD with full patch (12.4%). This work addresses a key limitation of single-signal reinforcement learning and on-policy self-distillation for software engineering agents by providing stage-specific guidance, which could lead to more effective training of code-repair agents. The significant pass@1 improvements on SWE-bench Verified suggest that decomposing the repair process into stages with tailored supervision is a promising direction for the AI-for-code community. The method uses a rule-based router to assign each step of an end-to-end rollout to a stage based on its tool call, with a frozen teacher seeing only the matching evidence (changed files/lines for localization, fail-to-pass tests for reproduction, diff for patching). Reversing the stage order under R2E-Gym reduces pass@1 to 11.4%, highlighting the importance of the progressive repair order.

**Background**: Software engineering agents are LLM-based systems that autonomously resolve repository-level issues by localizing faulty code, reproducing failures, and generating patches. Researchers propose MORE, a self-evolving training framework that adaptively selects both the reasoning form (direct answer, short/long chain-of-thought, or code-based reasoning) and the computational effort for each task. It uses a two-stage paradigm: Stage 1 builds a compact prior over reasoning modes, and Stage 2 self-evolves this prior with Mode-Adaptive and Test-time Effort PPO (MATE-PPO) on generated, verifiable task streams without curated data. This work addresses a known inefficiency in self-evolving agent training, where costly deliberation is applied uniformly across all tasks. By learning to allocate concise reasoning to easy tasks and extended deliberation only where useful, MORE could influence research on efficient reasoning and adaptive computation in LLM agents. MORE achieves consistent performance gains on coding, mathematics, and general-reasoning benchmarks across Base and Coder backbones at model scales from 3B to 14B. During inference, it demonstrates higher accuracy and better efficiency, with markedly shorter response lengths and reduced inference time.

Researchers present PACE, a research-proof agent that couples problem formulation with proof development through a structured research loop, and introduce ResearchProofBench, an applied-mathematics benchmark with 51 known-proof tasks (331 hidden checkpoints) and six open-problem cases. On the known-proof tasks, PACE achieves an aggregate Proof Score of 75.16 and completes 20 proofs, while in conjecture research its submissions receive higher review scores than baselines. PACE uses an independent verifier to check proofs against the original target and an evidence-tracking memory that stores assumptions and dependencies, marking evidence for revalidation when a candidate or condition changes. This memory supports task-specific context composition that keeps checked premises, exploratory material, and unresolved obligations distinct; the work is an arXiv preprint with no community discussion yet.

## [Iris framework enables order-invariant typed decisions over visual candidates with cache reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33702) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Iris, a framework that extends typed decision-making from text to image, text, or hybrid candidates while preserving order invariance and exact cache reuse. On a new visual-candidate benchmark built from Multimodal-Mind2Web (K=16), their conditioned-encoding design achieves 91.7/86.5/90.0% accuracy at one-third the latency of OneJev, and reusing image candidates cuts latency by 37x at K=256 and 191x at K=2048. This work addresses a key gap in multimodal agent systems: prior System One decision models guaranteed order invariance and cache reuse only for text candidates, while naive joint encoding of visual candidates is fast but unstable under reordering. Iris shows these guarantees can be preserved for visual candidates, which matters for UI element selection, product recommendation, and chart matching in production agents where candidate order changes and repeated images are common. Independent per-candidate encoding (Iris) achieves 78.4/72.1/74.8% accuracy with zero-flip rate under reordering, while joint encoding reaches 90.6/89.5/91.6% but suffers an 8–10% answer-flip rate when shuffled; the proposed conditioned encoding without inter-candidate cross-attention bridges this gap with strict order invariance and forked cache sharing. The paper also reports Iris-4B reaching 100% on JevBench original and easy, outperforming 30B MetaEncoder and 27B OpenJev, and a systems fix reformulating Qwen3.5 patch-embedding Conv3d as an exact matrix product for a 350x speedup on Ampere GPUs.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Typed decision-making tasks require a model to choose one option from a discrete set of candidates, such as selecting a UI element or matching a chart. Prior 'System One' models encode the request and each candidate separately, which makes the decision invariant to candidate order and allows candidate encodings to be cached and reused across requests. Extending this to multimodal settings is harder because visual candidates are typically encoded jointly with the request, breaking both order invariance and cache reuse. Multimodal-Mind2Web is a web-navigation benchmark whose multimodal variant supplies realistic visual candidates for such evaluations.

## [Entropy-Based Metric Detects Black-Box LLM Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33767) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.33767) proposes the Relative Peak Prominence Rate (RelPPR), an entropy-trajectory metric that detects black-box LLM-generated text by capturing sharp, localized entropy fluctuations characteristic of machine writing. The method achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot detection performance, particularly on instruction-conditioned inputs where existing dual-model and resampling-based detectors catastrophically fail. This work addresses a critical failure mode in LLM text detection—instruction-conditioned text in black-box settings—which is increasingly common in real-world applications like chatbots and writing assistants. RelPPR offers an interpretable, zero-shot alternative that could improve AI safety and misuse mitigation without requiring access to the source model. RelPPR builds on the Peak Prominence Rate (PPR), which averages the prominence of local peaks along the entropy trajectory, and normalizes it to capture structural contrast between human and machine text. The method is evaluated across diverse model families and datasets, and code is available on GitHub, though it remains an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Zero-shot detection of machine-generated text aims to identify LLM output without training on labeled data, which is crucial as LLMs become more fluent. Black-box detection assumes the source model is unknown, making it harder than white-box settings where model internals are accessible. Prior state-of-the-art methods include dual-model detectors (comparing outputs of two models) and resampling-based detectors (perturbing text and measuring probability changes), but these struggle when text is conditioned on instructions. Recent studies suggest human writing has a steady information flow (uniform entropy), while machine text shows sharp entropy fluctuations, motivating entropy-based detection.

A new arXiv paper (2610.33775) presents a comprehensive, practitioner-oriented guide to System 1 decision models—architectures that map inputs directly to typed, structured decisions in a single forward pass. It proposes a five-family taxonomy (encoder-based classifiers, reward models, non-autoregressive decision engines, contrastive decision models, and extraction models) and covers training methods, deployment trade-offs, and calibration theory. LLMs are slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated for routine sub-second decisions like routing, gating, scoring, and classification, so this guide addresses a real gap for engineers building efficient AI systems. Its focus on calibration and cascaded System 1 + System 2 workflows could shape how production agentic systems balance latency, cost, and reliability. The guide spans 190 references, covers 18 application domains, and maps an open-source ecosystem with over 70 model reproductions in weeks, including runnable code, a model zoo, a practitioner's checklist, and 22 self-assessment questions. It develops proper scoring rules theory, analyzes Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), and examines phenomena such as IIA violations, ordinal-scale bias, and few-shot recalibration under distribution shift.

## [ReLF: Rectified Flow Language Model Beats Autoregressive Baselines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33811) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce Rectified Language Flow (ReLF), a non-autoregressive language model that transports noise to token embeddings using rectified flow. With 64 function evaluations on OpenWebText, ReLF achieves lower generative perplexity than autoregressive baselines at matched diversity across all three model sizes tested. This work demonstrates that continuous flow-based language models can match or exceed the quality of autoregressive models, potentially enabling much faster parallel text generation. After two reflow rounds, ReLF generates 1,024-token sequences 15-19 times faster than autoregressive baselines at batch size 1, which could significantly impact deployment efficiency for large language models. ReLF combines fixed token embeddings constructed with Hellinger-SVD, self-conditioning guidance trained with cross-entropy, and regularized reflow for few-step generation. It also introduces singular logits, which combine an analytically computed term driving commitment to a valid token embedding as noise vanishes with a bounded neural residual that learns contextual token preferences.

EnvLunch introduces a label-free warm-up stage that samples valid action trajectories in executable environments, executes them to obtain final observations, and trains a language-model agent to recover a functionally equivalent trajectory from only the final observation. This warm-up improves downstream agentic reinforcement learning by over 9 points on average across all training budgets, and with few labels the baseline needs 8 to 32 times as many annotated examples to match EnvLunch's smallest-budget accuracy. The method requires no human-written or model-generated task descriptions, and letting the environment alone define the task yields larger gains than having the model write its own tasks over the same environments. ## [New Benchmark Tests Whether LLMs Trust Imperfect Partners Appropriately](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34107) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces a 324-scenario benchmark across 23 collaboration categories to evaluate whether large language models exhibit calibrated trust—rationally deciding to rely on, verify, or assist imperfect human or AI partners. Evaluating seven models alongside 36 controlled-history probes, the study finds that while the strongest frontier model approaches near-optimal decisions, most models fall short and display recurring pathologies. As LLMs increasingly collaborate with humans and other AI agents, the ability to calibrate trust—neither over-relying nor under-relying on imperfect partners—is critical for effective and safe multi-agent systems. This benchmark provides a rigorous analytical framework to measure this capability, highlighting a gap that could affect the reliability of AI-assisted decision-making in real-world deployments. Each scenario involves three sequential decisions with explicit transition dynamics, feedback emissions, and cost schedules, enabling exact analytical evaluation against expected consequences. The study dissociates evidence sensitivity from normatively appropriate action, finding that models often procure excessive safeguards, purchase verification tests with zero expected value of information, prioritize immediate savings over cooperative learning, and misallocate assistance; supplying explicit posterior distributions resolves some errors but introduces new failure modes.

**Background**: Calibrated trust refers to the rational adjustment of reliance on a partner as empirical evidence about their reliability accumulates. ## [Higher reasoning effort can hurt LLM agent performance, study finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34491) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.34491) empirically measures the counterfactual effect of reasoning effort levels on proprietary and open-weight models across four benchmarks, finding that higher effort frequently fails on tasks that lower effort solved and can cost up to 42x more on easy tasks. The authors frame reasoning effort as a credence good, since users cannot assess the marginal value of the computation they paid for even after a successful run. This challenges the common assumption that selecting the highest reasoning effort is always best, showing it is cost-inefficient and offers no guarantee of better instance-level performance. The findings affect anyone deploying LLM agents, from developers tuning inference-time compute budgets to organizations managing API costs. Effort changes not only token counts but also agent behavior: at higher effort, agents verify their own work more heavily and more often search for solutions rather than working through problems directly, lengthening trajectories without necessarily changing outcomes. A simple alternative—starting at the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure—matches or improves on fixed top effort across all models and benchmarks at lower cost for most proprietary models.

This paper applies that lens to reasoning effort, arguing users cannot tell whether the extra computation they purchased was actually necessary.

A new arXiv paper (2610.34553) systematically measures the minimum transformer dimension needed to perfectly memorize random factual triples, finding that this minimum dimension grows logarithmically with the number of facts N. ## [CSI-TextBench: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Language-Grounded WiFi Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34616) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CSI-TextBench introduces a large-scale dataset and benchmark that aligns WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) sensing data with natural language descriptions, unifying 3 sensing benchmarks into 285,790 samples across 7 tasks and pairing them with 2,291 hierarchically structured descriptions to construct 2.0 million CSI-text training tuples. The paper benchmarks 5 alignment methods from 4 paradigm families, showing that contrastive CSI-text alignment matches supervised classifiers without class labels, adapts to unseen classes with few samples, and responds to open-vocabulary prompts, with a single unified model achieving 86.9% top-1 accuracy on 140 composite scenes. This work bridges the gap between ambient WiFi sensing and language-driven AI systems, enabling ubiquitous indoor context awareness without cameras and potentially advancing privacy-preserving smart homes, assisted living, and smart buildings. It provides a much-needed resource for multimodal alignment research in a domain that lacks naturally paired text data. The dataset is constructed by deriving descriptions from labels rather than free-form human annotations, which may limit linguistic diversity, and the benchmark focuses on classification-style tasks rather than continuous sensing regression. The unified model's 86.9% top-1 accuracy on composite scenes outperforms task-specific classifier ensembles, but evaluation is confined to the 7 included tasks.

## [InferPriv Benchmark Reveals Inferential Privacy Leakage in LLM Assistants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34640) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces InferPriv, a benchmark that measures inferential privacy leakage—where an LLM assistant's reply contains indirect cues that let an honest-but-curious recipient infer sensitive user attributes. Evaluating five frontier models, the authors find that even with a privacy-aware system prompt, GPT-6.1-Sol, Sonnet-5.5, and Gemini-3.8-Flash achieve near-zero direct leakage but still exhibit inferential leakage rates of 16.2–25.2%. This work shows that existing privacy evaluations focusing only on explicit leakage can substantially understate the risks posed by LLM personal agents, which increasingly handle everyday tasks with access to private user data. It highlights the need for new evaluation standards and mitigation strategies as agents communicate with third parties on users' behalf. The benchmark models an honest-but-curious recipient who follows protocol but tries to infer sensitive attributes from routine task replies. The finding that inferential leakage persists at 16.2–25.2% across models and prompts, despite near-zero direct leakage under privacy-aware prompting, suggests that explicit leakage metrics alone are insufficient for assessing privacy risk.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: LLM-based personal agents are deployed to handle tasks like scheduling and communication, giving them access to private user information. Privacy research has traditionally focused on direct leakage, where a model explicitly states a secret, or on attacks like membership inference and training-data extraction. Inferential leakage is a subtler threat: the model never states the secret but leaves enough indirect cues for a recipient to deduce it. The honest-but-curious adversary model assumes a recipient who follows the protocol but tries to learn as much as possible from received messages.

## [Topic-Level Fairness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34683) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces topic-level fairness for RAG systems, showing that aggregate fairness metrics can mask per-topic disparities, and proposes a topic-specific reranker adaptation using Bradley-Terry preference pairs from generator outputs that reduces per-topic disparity by 40-51% while maintaining accuracy. This work reveals that RAG systems can appear fair overall while being unfair within specific topics, which could lead to biased information access for users querying different subjects. The proposed method offers a practical way to mitigate topic-level bias without sacrificing accuracy, impacting developers and deployers of RAG-based applications. The adaptation uses preference pairs built from the generator's own output to carry the direction that each topic requires, and with preference pairs from RoMQA alone, it reduces mean absolute per-topic disparity by 51% on RoMQA and 40% on TREC Fair Ranking. Notably, no baseline reaches this reduction even when modified to treat each topic separately, and using a single reranker for all topics also fails to achieve the same effect.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique where a large language model retrieves relevant information from external sources to ground its responses. Rerankers are second-stage components that reorder initially retrieved results to improve relevance. Group fairness in RAG typically measures whether a system treats different demographic groups equitably across all queries, but aggregating over queries can hide disparities that occur within specific topics. The Bradley-Terry model is a pairwise comparison framework often used to convert preferences into rankings, and here it is used to train rerankers with preference pairs derived from generator outputs.

## [Intervene, Calibrate, Discover: Causal Structure from Pixels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34711) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes a method that pairs image readouts with verified intervention values, uses a dimension-wise invertible calibration map to align visual responses with target settings, and then actively selects interventions to resolve graph directions and generate counterfactual images. It is evaluated on Domino, Pick-and-Place, Balance, Gears, CAUSAL3D, and CausalWorld benchmarks. This work addresses a key challenge in causal representation learning from pixels—misalignment between visual readouts and intervention values—and shows that active interventions can resolve orientation ambiguity that passive observations cannot. It has implications for building more reliable causal world models in vision-based reinforcement learning and robotics. The calibration map is learned with encoder and decoder frozen, and after freezing it, the agent selects interventions to fit local mechanisms; inverse calibration returns counterfactual states to the decoder's original coordinates. Controlled domino experiments show that interventions resolve orientation ambiguity left by equal additional observations, and calibration reduces mean error of predicted changes in other variables within the same factual context compared to an uncalibrated model.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Causal representation learning aims to recover high-level causal variables from low-level observations such as images, so that interventions and counterfactuals become well-defined. A central difficulty is that visual readouts may not align with the numerical values used in interventions, and passive observations often leave the direction of causal edges ambiguous. Active interventions can provide direct evidence about causal directions that observational data cannot.

The paper proposes prefetch-steered routing (PSR), which conditions MoE routing on a deterministic logical cache of prefetched experts, achieving 2.2-2.3x faster offloaded decoding on OLMoE-1B-7B compared to exact routing with LRU, while keeping outputs independent of transfer timing. ## [SciValidityBench tests whether scientific agents know when remembered facts are valid to use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34767) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced SciValidityBench, an executable benchmark factory with 64 TaskSpecs spanning five validity modules and six scientific domains, designed to evaluate whether scientific agents can judge when a correctly remembered fact is valid to use in decisions rather than merely retrieving it. The SciStateForge compiler-reader framework turns distributed experimental histories into explicit decision-governing state, and across four model families compiled scientific state improved valid decision-making by 9.2–18.8 percentage points over a generic Event Graph. This work shifts agent-memory evaluation from finding the right fact to deciding whether that fact should control the decision, addressing a stricter and underexplored problem for scientific agents where a correctly remembered result may still be invalid to use. It could influence how memory systems for AI/ML agents are designed and benchmarked, particularly in high-stakes scientific and experimental contexts. TaskSpecs couple generated experimental histories with scientific-state definitions, programmatic decision oracles, controlled interventions, and automatic scoring, while counterfactual pairs and targeted corruption-repair controls test whether models use those dependencies and localize failures. Retrieval alone does not reproduce the cross-family gain, and content-identical flat and typed views show the improvement comes from exposing governing state rather than a particular graph serialization.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Agent-memory benchmarks typically frame long-term memory as a retrieval problem: can an agent recover the relevant record from a long and evolving history? Scientific agents face a stricter issue called scientific use validity—whether remembered evidence is eligible to influence a decision under the state governing its interpretation—since the same reported test result can support confirmation when the outcome and stopping rule were fixed in advance, yet only exploration when the outcome was selected from many inspected results. SciValidityBench is an early arXiv preprint (2610.34767) and has not yet been peer-reviewed.

## [Centralized Critics for N-Agent Ad Hoc Teamwork: Unbiased Advantage Estimators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34799) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper compares two classes of advantage estimators for centralized critics in N-agent ad hoc teamwork (NAHT): controlled history estimators, which condition only on the learner's own agents' histories, and joint history estimators, which also condition on uncontrolled teammates' histories. It proves both are unbiased and characterizes when joint history estimation achieves strictly lower variance, with experiments showing joint history critics match or outperform controlled ones in sample efficiency and final returns. This work provides the first theoretical justification and empirical recommendation for incorporating uncontrolled agent histories into centralized critics for ad hoc teamwork, addressing a gap in MARL where critic design for NAHT was poorly understood. It could guide more sample-efficient and robust training of agents that must coordinate with unknown teammates in dynamic real-world settings. The paper formally proves unbiasedness of both estimators and derives conditions under which the joint history estimator has strictly lower variance, though the analysis assumes access to teammates' histories during centralized training. Empirical results span a range of NAHT tasks, but the abstract does not specify the environments or the scale of N tested.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) is the dominant paradigm in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where agents learn using global information during training but act independently at execution. Ad hoc teamwork (AHT) refers to settings where an agent must cooperate with unknown teammates without pre-coordination; N-agent ad hoc teamwork (NAHT) extends this to multiple learning agents facing a dynamically varying set of uncontrolled teammates. Advantage estimation is a core component of policy gradient methods, measuring how much better an action is than the average, and the design of the centralized critic—what privileged information it uses—directly affects learning efficiency and stability.

## [TrustJev separates policy authority from untrusted evidence in LLM decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34826) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TrustJev is a new framework that combines protected policy scoring with bounded evidence corrections, using a single Transformer backbone to compute policy scores and a correction budget from trusted policy and candidates. A 0.6B implementation was evaluated against 14 baselines on three datasets, achieving the highest mean Balance and correctly answering all 32 attacks per source in 95.77% of sources in an authorization benchmark. This work addresses prompt injection and policy authority in LLM-based decision systems, a critical security concern as LLMs are increasingly used to select actions from natural language inputs. By bounding evidence corrections, TrustJev offers a concrete architectural approach to prevent untrusted external evidence from overriding application policies, which could improve safety in authentication, instruction hierarchy, and executable authorization tasks. The framework uses paired supervision to encourage stable predictions under instruction insertions that preserve task facts and changed preferences when edits change the correct answer, and authority supervision to accommodate evidence when the policy alone cannot determine the decision. It maintains comparable inference memory and median latency to baselines, with additional overhead primarily during training.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Prompt injection is a security risk where malicious instructions in input data attempt to override an application's intended behavior, exploiting the fact that LLMs do not clearly distinguish between developer instructions and user inputs. The instruction hierarchy is a framework that trains LLMs to prioritize privileged instructions (e.g., system messages) over lower-privileged ones (e.g., user messages and third-party inputs). TrustJev builds on these concepts by separating trusted policy authority from untrusted external evidence in decision models.

## [MONOLOGUE: Logic Hijacking Attack Poisons RAG with Single Document](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34829) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.34829) introduces MONOLOGUE, a single-document poisoning framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) that uses logic hijacking instead of explicit factual refutation. The attack concedes the ground truth as a historical baseline and then presents a counterfactual target as a recent record correction, with payloads refined offline via multi-dimensional gated optimization. This work shows that aligned LLMs can be manipulated without triggering guardrails by framing false information as a plausible update, making single-document poisoning a more stealthy and practical threat to RAG systems. It highlights the need for defenses that detect narrative manipulation, not just explicit contradictions. The attack was evaluated across three benchmarks, three retrieval backends, and four open-weight generator regimes, achieving the strongest overall attack efficacy among evaluated single-document poisoning attacks. Payloads are refined entirely offline using automated text quality audits and surrogate behavioral verification to avoid suspicious live writes.

## [REMAP Framework Measures Interaction-Induced Reasoning Alignment in Multi-Agent LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34836) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces REMAP (Reference-Entailment-Matrix for Agentic Process), a framework that quantifies how multi-agent LLM interaction produces reasoning alignment gains beyond matched individual self-refinement, validated across diverse model families and two multi-hop reasoning benchmarks. It also proposes a fact-level multi-agent communication framework that replaces full reasoning-trace exchange with compact, gap-aware, selectively routed information. This work provides a quantitative method to measure emergent alignment in multi-agent systems, linking interaction gains to peer-information recovery and revealing composition-dependent heterogeneity and asymmetric information transfer. It offers guidance for designing more effective and efficient multi-agent communication protocols, which is valuable for the multi-agent LLM research community. The framework uses Semantic Coverage and interaction-specific alignment gains to measure alignment, and experiments show that compact fact exchange improves reasoning alignment and task performance while reducing communication overhead. However, more selective communication exposes a trade-off between acquiring distributed information, retaining local content, and communication efficiency.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.34837) evaluates three vision-language-action (VLA) models on two video benchmarks, examining their internal representations and action tendencies when confronted with visible hazards. The study finds that task execution often remains the default response even when danger is internally registered, suggesting a gap between hazard perception and defensive action. This work highlights a critical safety gap in embodied AI: VLA models may continue executing tasks despite recognizing danger, which could lead to unsafe robot behavior in real-world deployments. It underscores the need for safety-aware action selection mechanisms beyond perception in robotics foundation models. The evaluation is limited to three models and two video benchmarks, and it focuses on stimulus-response framing inspired by biological defensive reactions. The finding that danger is internally registered but not acted upon suggests that safety interventions may need to target the action decoding stage rather than just perception.

## [DecoyCount benchmark reveals visual-reasoning misalignment in VLM counting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34855) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DecoyCount introduces a 1,660-image benchmark with designed decoys across seven mechanisms and paired prompts (neutral, alignment cue, and multi-hop scenario) to disentangle perception from reasoning errors in visual counting. Frontier vision-language models score below 50% accuracy, with reasoning-alignment gaps of 11.8–22.1 percentage points, and gaps often grow with more capable models, larger thinking budgets, and agentic processes. This benchmark shows that stronger general reasoning does not automatically translate to aligned visual reasoning, highlighting a substantial misalignment with human visual expectations that standard accuracy metrics miss. It provides a new metric and diagnostic tool for AI evaluation research, affecting how vision-language models are assessed and improved for real-world counting tasks. The benchmark uses paired prompts—a neutral question, a matched alignment cue, and a novel multi-hop, multi-image question—to measure the reasoning-alignment gap, defined as the accuracy difference when models are cue-guided versus unaided. A scenario-based multi-hop condition without explicit hinting did not improve aggregate performance, suggesting textual underspecification alone does not explain the misalignment.

## [UniGFM-RAG: End-to-End Graph Foundation Model and LLM Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34866) ⭐️ 7.0/10

UniGFM-RAG is a new end-to-end GraphRAG framework that tightly couples a graph foundation model (GFM) retriever with an LLM generator, using a fully differentiable graph bridge to convert retrieved node embeddings into soft-weighted graph prefixes for joint optimization. It also introduces a semantic-guided distillation module that uses pseudo-labels from query-document similarities to reduce reliance on expensive human annotations. This work addresses two key limitations of existing GraphRAG systems—decoupled retrieve-then-generate pipelines that misalign retrieval and reasoning, and the high cost of annotating training data for GFM retrievers—potentially enabling more accurate and scalable multi-hop question answering over graph-structured knowledge. It is relevant to researchers and practitioners building retrieval-augmented generation systems that need to integrate structured knowledge with LLMs. The graph bridge projects node embeddings into soft-weighted graph prefixes according to retrieval scores and combines them with raw document texts to form graph-augmented prompts, allowing the final answer loss to back-propagate through the bridge and jointly optimize retrieval and reasoning. Experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets and three out-of-domain GraphRAG benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines, though the abstract does not specify model sizes or computational costs.

## [GADAR: Cross-Domain Generalization for Classical Planning via Action Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34868) ⭐️ 7.0/10

GADAR introduces a policy that takes a domain description as input and constructs grounded actions in unseen planning domains without search, using a three-layer architecture of lifted domain, binding, and chain layers. In leave-one-domain-out experiments over eight benchmark domains, a single GADAR policy trained on seven domains solves 58.3% of test instances, nearly matching the 59.3% of dedicated single-domain models, and achieves 22.6% zero-shot coverage on held-out domains versus 3.3% for random choice. This work addresses a key limitation of learned planning policies—their inability to execute on new domains with different predicates and action schemas—by enabling a single network to run on any domain. It could significantly advance cross-domain generalization research in classical planning and reduce the need for domain-specific retraining. The architecture describes symbols by their structural roles rather than names, with the chain layer encoding which schema produces what another needs and how far each schema is from the goal. Zero-shot coverage remains well below in-domain coverage on most domains, and the paper analyzes where it is weakest, though it reaches 68% on held-out Visitall.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Classical planning involves finding a sequence of actions to reach a goal from an initial state, typically described in PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language). Learned policies can act without search but are usually tied to a specific domain because their network modules or parameters are designed per action schema or predicate. Lifted planning operates on parameterized schemas, while grounded planning works with fully instantiated actions; GADAR bridges these by embedding domain structure into the state graph.

## [ThinkBit: Two-Bit Quantization That Preserves LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34886) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ThinkBit introduces a strictly scalar two-bit quantization framework that assigns each layer a ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit tier based on a sensitivity metric, then searches codewords block by block with Gumbel-softmax and recalibrates scales via knowledge distillation. On Qwen3-1.7B, its recalibrated checkpoint scores 46.7 on MATH-500 versus 30.0 for EfficientQAT, and 73.0 after quantization-aware training, while at 0.52 GB it is smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the model. Reasoning models generate thousands of tokens per answer, so memory bandwidth dominates inference cost, and storing weights in two bits instead of bfloat16 could make inference up to 8× cheaper. ThinkBit shows that aggressive 2-bit compression can preserve difficult reasoning tasks rather than just perplexity or multiple-choice accuracy, which matters for deploying large reasoning models on constrained hardware. The framework uses a layerwise scheme that does not capture inter-layer interactions, so it recalibrates scales with codewords frozen using a distillation loss, then runs a short QAT stage and selects the final checkpoint via a paired reasoning test. It scales to 14B, where a 3.74 GB model scores 94.8 on MATH-500 versus 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model, though this is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Quantization reduces the precision of neural network weights, typically from 16-bit floating point to 2-4 bit integers, to shrink model size and speed up inference. Scalar quantization stores each weight as an integer codeword multiplied by a shared floating-point scale, which is compatible with standard inference kernels, unlike vector quantization. Gumbel-softmax is a relaxation technique that allows gradient-based optimization over discrete choices such as codeword assignments, and quantization-aware training (QAT) fine-tunes the model after quantization to recover accuracy.

The study releases the corpus pipeline, protocol, and code, and highlights two negative findings: the intrinsic SSL loss is not a valid selection criterion (a server-momentum sweep moves downstream macro-F1 by up to 0.29 while SSL loss varies by only 0.021), and transfer is highly sensitive to the backbone learning rate (the same checkpoint yields 0.169 or 0.829 macro-F1 on CWRU depending on a single order of magnitude). It bridges multi-agent reinforcement learning and LLM agent research, with potential impact on complex collaborative tasks requiring efficient communication. BCMAAC maintains beliefs over contextual information to facilitate training in decentralized settings where agents execute independently with limited communication and must infer useful information from communication traces. The improvements are especially notable in multi-turn tasks with richer contextual information, highlighting the advantage of belief modeling.

## [NeSySpec: Neuro-Symbolic Audit Framework for Engineering Specifications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35403) ⭐️ 7.0/10

NeSySpec is an interpretable neuro-symbolic audit framework built on Logic Tensor Networks that diagnoses violated physical constraints, identifies altered fields via abduction, and proposes minimum-change corrections in engineering specifications. It was validated on 107 aircraft types, with 16 test aircraft from 9 families held out, achieving 94.2% accuracy in naming violated constraints on corrupted records versus 79.5% for classical Fellegi-Holt diagnosis. This work demonstrates a practical neuro-symbolic approach to auditing complex engineering specifications, combining differentiable reasoning with abductive inference to provide interpretable diagnostics and corrections. It could impact quality assurance and verification processes in aerospace and other safety-critical domains where specification errors are costly. The framework uses differentiable graded predicates whose tolerances are learned from real records, and it abstains when evidence is missing, tying image evidence to described parts. On edits labeled from the edit alone without retraining, abduction finds the altered field in 59.3% of records, compared to 30.6% for minimum-cardinality localization with random tie-breaking.

## [Denoising Trajectory Concentration Predicts Lower Endpoint Uncertainty in Masked Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35425) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.35425) investigates whether convergence within denoising trajectories of masked diffusion language models is associated with lower uncertainty in their final outputs. Across 32,000 denoising trajectories from four models on four reasoning benchmarks, the authors find that stronger within-run concentration is associated with lower endpoint entropy (β = -0.222, p < 10^-25), and that features from a single denoising run can predict whether independent held-out runs will concentrate on a common endpoint or produce competing endpoints. This work links the internal dynamics of individual denoising runs to variability across repeated inference, offering a potential route to estimating endpoint-distribution properties with fewer complete generations. That could make uncertainty quantification for diffusion language models cheaper and more practical, which matters for deploying such models in high-stakes settings. The relationship is asymmetric: high within-run concentration almost exclusively accompanies concentrated endpoint distributions, whereas lower concentration occurs under both concentrated and competing endpoint regimes. The association persists for multi-token outputs and when reweighting positive-entropy cases, and it strengthens as denoising proceeds.

This paper asks whether information from the denoising trajectory itself—how stably the eventual output resolves during denoising—can serve as a cheaper signal of endpoint uncertainty.

## [LLM Explanations of Multimodal Dementia Prognosis Fail When Modalities Are Missing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35430) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper investigates whether LLM-based explanations of multimodal dementia prognosis remain faithful when costly modalities are missing, identifying phantom attribution and unfaithful narration as key failure points. Using 307 ADNI participants, the study found that all five missing-data strategies assigned 12% to 23% of attribution to unobserved modalities, and up to 45% when four modalities were absent. This work is significant because LLMs are increasingly used to translate model attributions into clinical narratives, and unfaithful explanations under missing data could mislead clinicians and harm patient care. It provides concrete failure modes and empirical evidence that missingness-aware strategies can reduce phantom attribution without sacrificing accuracy, which is valuable for both explainable AI and clinical AI communities. Across 51,200 reports from four language models and four prompting regimes, naming absent modalities in the prompt raised acknowledgement from 48% to 88% and cut phantom evidence twenty-fold, but advice on whether acquiring a missing test would change the prediction was correct in only 27% to 41% of cases until checked against executed restorations, which raised accuracy to 69% for open-weight narrators and 99.9% for a proprietary model. Higher phantom attribution was associated with more phantom evidence and fewer faithful direction claims, and narrators told to name absent modalities sometimes declared observed ones absent, an error that a structured template eliminated.

## [Omni-InteractScope benchmarks proactive agentic interaction in omnimodal streams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35439) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Omni-InteractScope, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups, designed to evaluate how omnimodal LLMs proactively intervene in continuous audiovisual streams. Experiments on 12 models revealed three key limitations: timely tool invocation is unreliable (at most 40% on-time first responses and 32.0% joint timing-and-tool accuracy), query-free reminder recall never exceeds 23.0%, and nine models cover none of the 26 end-to-end guidance sequences. This benchmark addresses a genuinely under-evaluated capability—proactive, agentic assistance over streaming multimodal input—and provides concrete, quantified evidence that current omnimodal LLMs struggle with timely action and sustained guidance. It will be valuable for the multimodal and agent-evaluation communities, highlighting the gap between passive multimodal understanding and reliable real-time assistance. The benchmark links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Targeted controls show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding, and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency.

A new arXiv perspective paper (2610.35453) proposes Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS), a framework that shifts from data aggregation to experience aggregation by having distributed AI agents share abstracted reasoning trajectories instead of raw data or model parameters. The paper outlines architectural principles, deployment considerations, governance requirements, and open challenges for this collaborative medical AI ecosystem. This conceptual shift could enable clinical AI to learn from diverse, distributed expertise without centralizing sensitive patient data or homogenizing model architectures, potentially improving adaptability to longitudinal patient care. If adopted, it could influence how healthcare institutions collaborate on AI, moving beyond the limitations of federated learning in handling heterogeneous clinical reasoning. Unlike federated learning, which averages numerical gradients across homogeneous model architectures, DAS exchanges structured records of clinical reasoning—sequences of observations, hypotheses, tool invocations, and outcome feedback. As a perspective paper, it lacks empirical validation, so practical feasibility and scalability remain to be demonstrated.

## [StaR-TTA adapts LLM confidence after agentic RL without labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35500) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.35500) shows that trajectory-based confidence estimators for LLMs degrade substantially after agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL) due to shifts in reasoning trajectories. The authors discover that a stability-reliability relationship persists across Base and RL models—more stable trajectories remain more likely to yield correct answers—and use it to build StaR-TTA, a label-free test-time confidence adaptation framework that achieves an average AUROC of 0.721 across four QA benchmarks. Confidence estimation is critical for deploying LLM agents safely, and this work reveals that a common post-training step (Agentic RL) can silently break existing estimators. StaR-TTA offers a practical, label-free fix that transfers across datasets, model families, scales, and RL algorithms, which matters for anyone building reliable agentic systems. StaR-TTA jointly learns from correctness supervision and stability-derived reliability supervision on labeled Base trajectories, then at test time reuses stability-induced reliability rankings from unlabeled RL trajectories to adapt confidence scores without target correctness labels. The method is evaluated on four QA benchmarks and shows consistent improvements across unseen datasets, model families and scales, and different Agentic RL algorithms.

Researchers introduced Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering (CANS), a unified, training-free framework that computes closed-form neuron-wise scaling coefficients to control target behaviors in LLMs while limiting general-capability loss. On Qwen3-4B, CANS reduced HarmBench attack success from 15.50% to 1.75% with only a 1.11-point average capability drop, outperforming SFT, CAA, and neuron-level baselines across safety, toxicity, and hallucination control tasks. CANS uses two proxies—log-probabilities of target tokens in model-generated responses and output-distribution KL divergence on general-purpose inputs—and combines their local approximations to derive a closed-form solution, avoiding iterative training or extra inference-time computation. A shared data-construction and intervention procedure enables cross-domain adaptation using sampled responses with target-behavior filtering and target-span annotations.

## [VaLoP improves reward-guided diffusion via value gradient lookahead and pullback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35607) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VaLoP introduces a value gradient lookahead and pullback technique that reduces estimation errors in reward-guided diffusion sampling by evaluating the value at a less noisy state one sampler step ahead and pulling its gradient back to the current state. The method also includes VaLoP-Fast, which amortizes the correction with a small head trained on a single reward and reused for others, and both variants outperform existing value-gradient guidance across models, rewards, and benchmarks. This work provides a theoretical insight that both common gradient estimators suffer from posterior covariance errors that grow with noise, and offers a practical fix that improves target reward performance without retraining the diffusion model. It could benefit AI/ML researchers working on reward-guided generation for images and actions, including text-to-image models and robot policies. VaLoP computes the required correction through the generator with one vector-Jacobian product, while VaLoP-Fast amortizes it with a small head that, for text-to-image models, is trained with a single reward and reused for others at about the cost of learned-value guidance. Both methods extend to critic-guided robot policies, with VaLoP-Fast achieving the highest success rates on LIBERO and RoboCasa benchmarks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Reward-guided diffusion steers a pretrained diffusion or flow model toward outputs preferred by a reward model at sampling time, without retraining for each reward, by following the gradient of a value function (the expected reward given the noisy state). Common estimates of this gradient—through a one-step denoised estimate or via learned value models—are least accurate at high noise levels, where the coarse structure of the sample is decided. The paper identifies these errors as posterior covariances that grow with uncertainty about the clean sample, and proposes lookahead to a less noisy state to reduce them.

## [Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35865) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper presents a geometrical interpretation of the evolution strategies (ES) update, showing that the mean-subtracted update equals the displacement of the reward-weighted center of mass from the centroid, scaled by a factor depending on the mean reward, for any finite population. This provides a novel intuitive visualization of ES updates, which could lead to new algorithmic insights or improvements in evolutionary optimization methods. The physical interpretation requires nonnegative rewards, which can always be achieved by adding a constant to all rewards without changing the update; in the limit of large populations or under antithetic sampling, the centroid coincides with the model, simplifying the interpretation to moving toward the reward-weighted center of mass.

**Background**: Evolution strategies (ES) are a class of evolutionary algorithms that optimize by sampling perturbed copies of a model, evaluating their rewards, and updating in the reward-weighted direction. Traditionally, this update is viewed as an estimate of a smoothed gradient. The paper offers an alternative geometric perspective using concepts of center of mass and centroid.

Researchers introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), an unsupervised trajectory-level metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning, to measure behavioral inconsistency across independent LLM agent rollouts. RSD recursively estimates expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two rollouts from the same state using natural language inference, and when used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, it reduces variation in task progress from 132% to 91% on tau2-bench and from 90% to 44% on toolsandbox. LLM agents with tool use often behave inconsistently across runs, which undermines deployment reliability, yet existing metrics mainly measure task correctness rather than consistency. RSD fills this gap by providing a turn-level consistency score that can also serve as a reward signal, potentially improving agent reliability without requiring ground-truth labels. RSD is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts, allowing it to estimate future divergence from the current state without needing the full trajectory to complete. Training with RSD as an additional reward signal matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance and improves performance across benchmarks and model scales.

A new arXiv paper (2610.33016) shows that the pre-tokenizer regex used by Llama-3 and Qwen3 splits Devanagari words at vowel signs, causing Nepali text to consume 2.6–5.8x more tokens than equivalent English text. The authors propose a small regex edit that provably preserves all existing token IDs for text without combining marks or Devanagari characters, and with 32,000 new merges reduces the Nepali-to-English token ratio to 1.01, about 54% fewer Nepali tokens than standard merge-based extension. This identifies a concrete, underappreciated tokenizer bug that affects multilingual LLM efficiency for Devanagari-script languages, which are spoken by hundreds of millions of people. The fix is provably English-preserving and could be adopted by model developers to reduce inference costs and improve effective context length for Nepali and related languages. Merge-based vocabulary extension cannot fully repair the split because no number of new merges brings the Nepali token premium below about 2.2 for Llama-3 and Qwen3, and ten released extensions already end within 4% of this pre-token floor. In small-budget continued pretraining of Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen3-0.6B, the original tokenizer gave the lowest held-out Nepali bits per byte under every recipe tested, and matching training steps reversed the order on Qwen but not on Llama; whether token savings yield favorable latency and quality trade-offs in generation remains untested.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Most modern LLMs use subword tokenizers like BPE, which first split text into words using a pre-tokenization regular expression and then apply learned merges. Devanagari, the script used for Nepali and Hindi, is an abugida where vowel signs are combining marks attached to consonants; if the regex only matches Unicode letters, it breaks words at these marks. Merge-based vocabulary extension adds new tokens to an existing tokenizer to better cover a target language, but it operates after pre-tokenization and thus cannot rejoin pieces that were already split.

## [Harness Skills Help Strong LLMs but Harm Weak Ones, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33024) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.33024) shows that harness self-evolution skills are not uniformly beneficial across model capabilities: across seven models and three benchmarks, 103 task-skill pairs improved GPT-5.6-luna by 31.1 points but degraded Gemma-4-E4B by 8.8 points. The authors propose skill adaptation, distilling failure diagnoses into a fixed meta-skill that guides a rewriter (Kimi-K3) to reformulate skills for weaker executors, yielding 5.1–14.1 point gains over original skills and 2.0–5.1 point gains in a five-round self-evolution loop. This work highlights a real and underexplored pitfall in LLM agent self-evolution: skills that boost strong models can actively harm weaker ones, so harness design must account for executor capability. The findings offer practical guidance for building more robust and equitable self-evolving agent systems, affecting researchers and practitioners deploying agents across heterogeneous model sizes. In 86% of failed weak-model runs, the violated requirement was already stated in the skill, indicating the issue is executability rather than missing knowledge. The meta-skill is distilled from diagnoses of failures in tool execution, context management, instruction following, and verification, and the adaptation can work without execution evidence when guided by a capable external rewriter.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: An agent harness is the runtime scaffolding around an LLM that turns it into an agent—driving model and tool calls, managing context, and applying policies. Harness self-evolution lets agents improve by updating this external harness from execution experience without changing model parameters. Skills are persistent guidance artifacts (e.g., SKILL.md files) that the harness injects to steer the model's behavior.

## [Conceptizer adds concept-level reward to next-token prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33027) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Conceptizer introduces a training framework that extends next-token prediction with a reward for meaning, using a fixed vocabulary of ~9K concepts built from contextual synonyms. Applied to 3 model families at 1B-8B parameters, it achieves the lowest held-out NTP perplexity at concept-target positions and improves downstream performance on knowledge and sentiment tasks. This work suggests that language models can be directly optimized to predict meaning rather than only exact next tokens, potentially leading to better generalization and more robust representations. It offers a parameter-free way to inject semantic supervision into standard training, which could influence future LLM training objectives. The concept vocabulary is fixed and model-agnostic, so no additional model parameters are introduced. The method maps each next-token distribution to a concept distribution and shares the reward for the target meaning across its possible wordings, but it remains an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Most large language models are trained with next-token prediction (NTP), which rewards only the token that actually occurs next and penalizes all alternatives, even valid synonyms. Perplexity is a standard metric for evaluating how well a model predicts held-out text. Conceptizer builds on the idea that natural language often offers many ways to express the same meaning, using contextual synonyms to define concept units alongside tokens.

## [LLM-written lessons can carry chance into agent decisions, study finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33029) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A pre-registered study with 256 synthetic worlds and 90,084 answers from 11 LLM endpoints found that when a more reliable tool failed by chance, lessons written by ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction caused agents to choose the worse tool in 11.6% of next runs, compared to 0.4% with an irrelevant memory item. This reveals a subtle failure mode in self-improving agents: noisy outcomes can be encoded into lessons that bias future tool choices, undermining the reliability of memory-based learning systems that are increasingly deployed in production. The effect was larger when the log did not state that failures are independent (+0.181) than when it did (+0.042), and a three-sentence decision-quality note in the writing instruction reduced the worse-tool rate to 7.5%, though neither mitigation met the pre-registered harm-reduction rule at every endpoint.

**Background**: Self-improving LLM agents often use memory frameworks like ReasoningBank to distill lessons from past runs and reuse them in future decisions. When outcomes are noisy, a lesson may incorrectly attribute success or failure to the tool used rather than to chance, propagating bias into later choices.

The paper introduces Parametric Session State, a reusable session-memory layer that remembers what to search for in long conversations while keeping factual knowledge external. It addresses the problem of retrieval intent in follow-up queries that omit key terms established many turns earlier. This approach decouples retrieval intent from factual knowledge, offering a cheaper alternative to replaying full history with long-context models or relying on explicit textual memory in conversational RAG. The method maintains a parametric memory of session state, avoiding the cost of processing history at each query, but details on architecture, training, and evaluation are not provided in the abstract. ## [Aerial-R1: Reinforcement Learning Boosts Aerial MLLM Reasoning and Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33056) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Aerial-R1 is the first aerial multimodal large language model (MLLM) framework to apply reinforcement learning, inspired by DeepSeek-R1, to reinforce visual reasoning for aerial reasoning and segmentation. It introduces Hybrid-View Group Advantage-Weighted Regression (H-GAWR), which constructs dynamic groups of high- and low-resolution views to bridge group-relative advantage estimation with advantage-weighted policy extraction, and is evaluated on VSAI-Ref, the first aerial MLLM benchmark for dense reasoning and hallucination robustness. Aerial MLLMs suffer from severe hallucination due to extreme scale variations and visual ambiguity, and existing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paradigms force models to mimic ground truth without modeling uncertainty, leading to blind guessing on tiny or unrecognizable objects. Aerial-R1's reinforcement learning approach with an explicit refusal mechanism significantly improves segmentation precision and mitigates fatal hallucinations, paving the way for more reliable and trustworthy aerial agents. H-GAWR adapts policy optimization for non-autoregressive mask generation by enforcing consensus on clear inputs and strictly penalizing hallucinations on ambiguous ones, thereby developing an explicitly incentivized refusal mechanism. The method is evaluated on VSAI-Ref, a new benchmark dedicated to jointly evaluating dense reasoning and hallucination robustness in aerial scenes, and code is available on GitHub.

## [MARC uses shared kinematic graph to correct articulated object code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33060) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MARC introduces a mechanism-aware reflective correction framework that shares an executable kinematic graph across program construction, motion solving, and correction to generate articulated objects that actually execute intended motion. On a 20-object test set, MARC with Kimi-K3 achieves 67.8% valid motion coverage and 60.0% overall success, outperforming six baselines, with correction improving scores by 13.7 and 20.0 percentage points from the same initial candidates. This work addresses the hard problem of closed-chain and coupled mechanisms in articulated object generation, where a single connection error can block motion or separate parts. It could enable more reliable generation of functional articulated objects for robotics and simulation, impacting researchers in code generation, kinematics, and LLM agents. The kinematic graph binds physical connections to local attachment frames and represents loop closures and joint-coordinate couplings, with a numerical solver computing follower motion and associating errors to specific connections and configurations. Ablations show the benefits of graph-based mechanism support and graph-guided repair, though the abstract is truncated and no community discussion is provided.

Closed-chain mechanisms contain loops of links, making their motion more constrained and error-sensitive than open-chain robots, and joint-coordinate coupling means the motion of one joint depends on another. Generating such mechanisms from images and text requires not only plausible parts but also ensuring the assembled mechanism can execute the intended motion.

## [Oddin enables latent visual reasoning in unified multimodal models via self-distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33062) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Oddin introduces a self-distillation framework that replaces intermediate images with compact latent tokens processed entirely by the understanding branch of a unified large multimodal model (ULMM), reserving the generation branch for the final output image. Trained with three objectives—final image generation loss, text distillation loss, and cross-entropy loss for special tokens—Oddin outperforms interleaved generation baselines and closed-source VLMs on average across seven VBVR-Pro visual reasoning tasks. This work shows that ULMMs can perform complex visual reasoning without generating intermediate images, potentially reducing computational overhead and enabling more efficient multimodal reasoning. It also bridges latent visual reasoning—previously limited to vision-language models incapable of image generation—with unified models that can both understand and generate images. Oddin uses offline self-distillation with latent tokens that attend to relevant regions in the input image, as shown by qualitative analysis. The approach is evaluated on seven VBVR-Pro tasks, but as an arXiv preprint it has not yet undergone peer review or community validation.

Latent visual reasoning instead uses compact latent tokens in a continuous embedding space to reason implicitly, but most existing methods rely on vision-language models that cannot generate images. ## [CANARY: A Training-Free Detector for Confident Failures in Image Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33063) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper identifies a structural blind spot in Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) for detecting confident failures and proposes CANARY, a training-free per-class kNN detector on PCA residuals of penultimate features. CANARY matches or improves MSP in 382 of 385 shift cells across five backbones, with worst-case regression within seed noise. This work provides a theoretical explanation for why a standard failure predictor fails and offers a practical, training-free solution that can be easily integrated into deployed vision systems. It is particularly valuable for safety-critical applications where silent high-confidence errors are costly. CANARY computes a per-class kNN distance on the PCA residual of penultimate features, percentile-calibrates on validation data, and fuses with MSP via a single validation-tuned weight. Its benefit follows a headroom law: gains grow as baseline MSP quality falls, and all parameters are selected on in-distribution data alone.

**Background**: Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) is a common baseline for detecting when a classifier is likely to be wrong, using the highest softmax output as a confidence score. However, MSP can be overconfident on out-of-distribution or shifted inputs, leading to silent failures. CANARY leverages the idea that off-manifold residuals in feature space, measured via PCA and kNN, capture class-conditional typicality that MSP misses.

## [PhaseBreak: Temporal Retiming Defense Against Unauthorized Image-to-Video Animation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33070) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PhaseBreak introduces a white-box adversarial perturbation method that protects shared images from unauthorized image-to-video (I2V) animation by retiming temporal feature events in diffusion denoisers rather than globally attenuating them. Evaluated on Stable Video Diffusion and DynamiCrafter, protected images produce greater short-term motion variation and lower temporal regularity, impeding stable motion customization. This work addresses a growing privacy concern: I2V models can animate anyone's portrait without consent, and PhaseBreak offers a proactive protection that preserves the normal image-sharing workflow. Its spectral retiming approach provides finer control over subtle or localized motion than existing spectral disruption objectives, potentially enabling more practical and robust defenses for individuals sharing images online. PhaseBreak operates along the true temporal axis and uses a subject-aware mask to confine the protective perturbation to the depicted subject, preserving the rest of the image. As a white-box method, it assumes access to the target I2V model's internals, which may limit its practical applicability against unknown or black-box models.

Proactive protection methods add imperceptible adversarial perturbations to images before sharing, aiming to disrupt downstream generation while keeping the image visually intact. Existing spectral disruption objectives globally attenuate temporal features, but they offer limited control over subtle or spatially localized motion. PhaseBreak builds on the insight that generated dynamics depend not only on feature strength but also on the temporal ordering of feature events in the denoiser.

## [AGQ: Action-Guided Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization for Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33074) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AGQ introduces an action-guided ultra-low-bit quantization method for vision-language-action (VLA) models, achieving 92.7% task success at W3 and 70.5% at W2.5 on the LIBERO benchmark, outperforming AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points at W3. It also presents an asymmetric W1.5* configuration that, with lossless coding, achieves 6.10× complete-model compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5% task success. VLA models are large and memory-hungry, making deployment on robots with constrained onboard memory difficult; AGQ shows that ultra-low-bit quantization can drastically reduce memory footprint while largely preserving task performance, which could enable more capable robots to run on edge hardware. The method's gains over established post-training quantization baselines like AWQ and GPTQ highlight the importance of action-aware bit allocation for embodied AI workloads. AGQ combines action sensitivity with a measured proxy for weight recovery cost to allocate matrix bitwidths under storage budgets, uses per-channel calibration to compensate for quantization error, and keeps a uniform bitwidth within each matrix to preserve regular layouts. It also employs bit-dependent grouped lossless coding to reduce resident weight storage and block-wise recovery to limit temporary buffers.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Vision-language-action (VLA) models take a natural-language instruction and an image observation as input and output low-level robot actions, combining vision-language model backbones with an action decoder. Quantization reduces the numerical precision of model weights (e.g., from 16-bit to 3-bit or lower) to shrink memory and compute costs, and post-training methods such as AWQ and GPTQ are widely used for large language models. Ultra-low-bit quantization (below 4 bits) is especially challenging because it can severely degrade accuracy, and VLA models add the complication that quantization errors may affect action sequences in ways that are not captured by standard language-model metrics.

AnalogPortBench introduces 54 tasks for porting ten analog circuits (from current mirrors to telescopic amplifiers) from a 0.18 µm process to the open-source SKY130 PDK, with tasks ranging from direct ports to reduced-supply and infeasible specifications. Every feasible task has a reference design verified at five process corners, ensuring robustness across PVT variations. The evaluation shows that simulation feedback yields larger gains than increasing sample count or reasoning level, and that models seldom flag infeasible specifications, a critical gap for practical deployment.

## [DocAuth uses attribution to improve LLM-generated documentation for formal libraries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33094) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces DocAuth, a method that checks whether a documentation statement depends on a function's specific behavior (attribution) and uses this to generate and validate natural-language documentation for formal libraries. On 150 functions from ACL2's Community Books, three LLMs produced provably true but non-attributable properties for about a third of the functions, and DocAuth raised the share of published sentences confirmed as attributable from 82.9% to 94.7% compared to a truth-only pipeline. This work shows that provable truth alone is insufficient for documentation quality, since a statement can remain true even after a function's behavior changes. Attribution provides a complementary criterion that could improve LLM-assisted documentation for formal libraries and help developers trust natural-language descriptions of verified code. DocAuth attaches to each published sentence the formal property recovered from it along with checkable evidence, and it matches or exceeds the attribution rate of a mutation-based filter while delivering 37% more attributable sentences. The evaluation is limited to 150 functions from ACL2's Community Books and relies on LLM-generated properties, so generalization to other formal systems remains to be tested.

**Background**: ACL2 is a theorem prover and programming language based on Common Lisp, widely used for software and hardware verification; its Community Books library contains many formally verified definitions and theorems. ## [EGGPlacer: Energy-Guided Diffusion for Thermal-Aware Chip Placement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33099) ⭐️ 7.0/10

EGGPlacer is a new energy-guided diffusion framework for chip macro placement that incorporates analytical placement feedback (standard cell distribution and a full netlist wirelength proxy) and differentiable thermal feedback into the reverse diffusion process without retraining the generative model. Experiments on public benchmarks show it achieves competitive mixed-size HPWL and the lowest average routed wirelength and peak temperature among evaluated methods. This work addresses a key limitation of learning-based macro placers, which typically optimize only macro-only HPWL and ignore standard cell connectivity and thermal effects. By integrating analytical and thermal feedback, it could lead to chip designs with better routability and thermal behavior, impacting EDA flows and physical design engineers. The guidance signals are formulated as composable energies injected throughout reverse diffusion, acting as an online physical response model without retraining. Ablation studies show that analytical and thermal guidance provide distinct and complementary benefits across wirelength proxies, routed wirelength, and thermal objectives.
