## [WhoWins benchmark reveals inconsistent instruction conflict resolution in LLM agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33201) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces the WhoWins benchmark, a controlled study with 1,080 code-scored scenarios across five task types and seven experiments that vary only how instructions are delivered. Testing 14 open-weight models (0.6B to 122B parameters, with thinking on and off) over 1,887,356 scored replies, the study finds that instruction conflicts are resolved inconsistently, with position, role, and label effects varying across models and task types. This work challenges the assumption that instruction hierarchy alone determines which conflicting instruction an LLM agent follows, showing that surface features like position and labeling can outweigh source authority. The findings have direct implications for AI safety and reliability, especially for defending against prompt injection and ensuring agents prioritize trusted instructions. Within a single message, the first of two conflicting lines wins 72.42–94.66% of the time, but across messages this drops to 22.95–62.65%. A policy sent first in the system or developer message loses most conflicts with later lines in every Qwen model but wins most on gpt-oss when it acts, and at most 2.92% of decided pair replies explicitly flag or hedge a conflict.

**Background**: LLM agents receive instructions from multiple sources—system prompts, developer configuration, user requests, tool outputs, and saved memory—which often conflict. The standard defense is an instruction hierarchy that ranks sources by trust (e.g., system above developer above user above tool output), but a source simultaneously sets the instruction's position, chat role, and label, making it unclear which factor drives model behavior. Prompt injection attacks exploit this ambiguity by embedding malicious instructions in tool outputs or external data.

A new arXiv paper (2610.33312) introduces Probabilistic Agentic Programming (PAP), a paradigm that makes responsibility boundaries explicit programming abstractions connecting mandate, authority, effects, and evidence. It formalizes a mediation kernel with checks before tool execution, operation-bound approval, resource limits, and evidence, and provides inductive proofs of conditional safety for arbitrary model responses. As LLM agents increasingly combine reasoning, tools, memory, and delegation, authority is often scattered across prompts, host code, and configuration, making safety hard to guarantee. The paper compares PAP along seven dimensions and uses a backward simulation to match graph executions to source executions in a defined sequential Touba subset. An exploratory study with seven business cases, seven models from three providers, five methods, and five repetitions yielded 1,225 assessed observations; native Touba completed all 35 observations on six models and 30 on the remaining model, with all paired case intervals including zero.

## [Enclawed: Deterministic Security Runtime for LLM Agents on HPC Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33318) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Enclawed, a deterministic distributed security runtime that extends its single-user design to parallel HPC and agent swarms, using a hardware root of trust called Enclaweder to supervise every MPI rank. The system employs a launch gate, consensus-governed short leases with signed heartbeats, and per-rank supervisors that pause or kill jobs on lease lapse or tampering, all without administrator privileges and over SSH alone. The paper reports that none of 23 surveyed systems supervises running jobs or withstands a compromised control host, highlighting a critical gap in HPC security for LLM agent workloads. Enclawed's approach could protect expensive simulations and safety-critical results from forged outputs and malicious launches, affecting researchers and institutions running AI agents on shared clusters. Enclawed adds about 3 seconds of start-up overhead and leaves the compute loop of a 16-rank LAMMPS job unchanged, including on GPUs; in tests, 12 live attacks (including colluding coordinators) ended fail-closed, and a launch gate denied all 24 malicious launches while allowing 108 legitimate ones. The core and the HPC Agent Security Benchmark are open source, though the abstract is truncated and full validation details are limited.

## [Exact Unlearning Must Account for Data Deduplication in Training Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33426) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper formalizes exact unlearning for training pipelines that deduplicate data, showing that a deletion budget determines which records can still enter training and enabling exact repair of training statistics after repeated deletions. It also constructs finite-precision features for ridge regression, where allowing one more deletion changes the required private information from zero to every private feature sign in excluded candidates. This work addresses a subtle but important gap in machine unlearning: when training pipelines remove similar examples, deleting a raw record can change the selection and admit previously excluded data, complicating exact unlearning guarantees. It introduces a retention contract concept that could influence how privacy-preserving services design data retention and deletion policies. The paper uses a fixed rule where earlier similar records block later ones, and on 1,001 AskUbuntu development records, deleting an initially excluded record admits another record at 13 of 51 fixed similarity cutoffs, with exact membership repair passing 13,056 deletion-step checks. However, two model-based semantic calibrations fail their fixed criteria, so the downstream task study is not run.

## [First Finite-Time Bounds for Importance-Corrected Momentum Actor-Critic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33477) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper presents a unified analysis of an actor-critic method that combines a ridge-regularized pathwise LSTD critic with importance-corrected momentum (ICM) actors, establishing the first finite-time convergence bounds along a single Markovian trajectory. The averaged gradient norm over K updates is bounded by O(K^{-1/3} + 1/T) for normalized steps and O(K^{-1/4} + 1/T) for unnormalized steps, where T is the frame length. This provides the first theoretical convergence guarantees for ICM actor-critic methods, which are important for understanding the behavior of momentum-based policy optimization in reinforcement learning. The results specialize to popular optimizers like Muon, normalized SGD with momentum, SGD with momentum, and AdaNorm, offering insights into when orthogonalization outperforms normalization. The critic solves a ridge-regularized system per frame using Newton-Schulz inversion, requiring no stepsize, no knowledge of mixing time, and no rank condition. The analysis shows that with a dimension-free stepsize, Muon confines the factor min{m,n}^{1/2} associated with an m×n actor parameter matrix to the noise and correction terms, and orthogonalization guarantees a larger noiseless ascent than normalization exactly when the gradient's nuclear rank exceeds the spectral-to-Frobenius curvature ratio.

Momentum-based optimizers such as Muon use orthogonalization of gradients via Newton-Schulz iteration to accelerate training, but their theoretical convergence in reinforcement learning settings has been less understood.

Pacifo reduces the number of private layers and costly FHE operations by partitioning layers into public and private parts and approximating ReLU with polynomials, and it offers flexible security configurations to accommodate varying client privacy requirements. The paper introduces hybrid-time PINNs (HT-PINNs) that assign a separate neural network to each continuous flow interval of a hybrid system and jointly train these networks with the jump times and unknown parameters. In experiments, HT-PINNs successfully recovered the number of jumps and the restitution coefficient of a bouncing ball, and in a MuJoCo robotic disassembly simulation, they identified the jump sequence and estimated static and kinetic friction coefficients with errors of 0.1% and 1.7%. This work addresses a fundamental limitation of standard PINNs, which assume smooth temporal dynamics and thus fail on hybrid systems with discrete jumps. The approach could enable accurate learning and parameter identification for robotic contact tasks, impact dynamics, and other cyber-physical systems where discontinuities are inherent. The number of jumps and the sequence of modes are determined by enumeration, which may limit scalability to systems with many jumps.

Researchers introduced WorldFailBench, a new benchmark with three evaluation tasks—failure reason, failure stage, and failure boundary—that assesses whether world models faithfully reproduce how and at which stages robot policies fail, rather than only whether tasks succeed or fail. ## [ProbeID verifies MCP tool identity under registry drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33633) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ProbeID is a new verification method that compares canonicalized responses to schema-valid probes against a trusted admission reference to determine which implementation of an MCP tool an LLM agent actually invokes. It abstains under ambiguity and achieves 0.956 hit@1 on cached MCP-IdentityDrift cases, while description routers perform near chance. This addresses a real security gap in LLM agent tool selection, where copyable descriptions cannot guarantee which implementation runs, allowing squatters to impersonate tools. The approach uses independent probes and a fixed margin to achieve a probe budget logarithmic in the candidate count, bounding the joint probability of a wrong decision. However, simpler exact comparisons tie its performance, MMD better tolerates heavy value noise, and a 32B behavioral judge is similarly accurate at higher cost; verification depends on reference integrity, probe coverage, and response noise.

## [Audited Pivot Scoring Mechanism Incentivizes Truthful Confidence in LLM Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33728) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the Audited Pivot Scoring Mechanism (APSM), a mechanism-design approach that combines inverse-propensity-weighted sparse audits, Clarke pivot externality charges, and a strictly proper scoring rule to make truthful confidence reporting the unique expected-utility best response in LLM multi-agent systems where confidence determines downstream resource allocation. Experiments show that LLM agents inflate confidence under Top-K incentives, and APSM reduces distortion, enlarges the utility margin against allocation-changing deviations by 1.93×, and improves robustness under approximate execution compared to Compensated Proper Scoring (CPS). This work addresses a critical gap in AI alignment and multi-agent coordination: existing calibration methods assume passive reporting and ignore strategic incentives that arise when confidence determines resource allocation. By providing a mechanism-design solution with theoretical guarantees, it offers a principled layer for reliable elicitation of confidence in LLM-based systems, which could impact how multi-agent systems allocate attention, computation, and decision influence. APSM offsets platform-controlled allocation benefits, uses inverse-propensity-weighted sparse audits to reduce audit cost, charges the Clarke pivot externality, and applies a strictly proper score; under stated model assumptions, truthful reporting is the unique expected-utility best response. The paper also characterizes approximate execution and the audit-variance trade-off, and experiments show CPS achieves higher exact allocation match while APSM yields lower Brier loss and fewer cutoff crossings.

On a closed-loop protocol with real bioinformatics tools, ProtAgent-8B achieves 61.00% success under the annotation-coverage metric, compared with 41.60% for DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking 671B and 60.80% for the strongest evaluated frontier system. This shows that a small, post-trained model can outperform much larger frontier models on multi-step tool-use tasks in a specialized scientific domain, suggesting that interaction-level credit assignment can substitute for raw model scale. If the approach generalizes, it could make capable bioinformatics agents cheaper and more deployable for labs that cannot rely on frontier-scale inference. The key technical difference is that step-level returns assign rewards to the responses that produced them and to preceding actions, whereas an episode-level baseline assigns one episode return to every action; in a three-seed comparison, mean success is 42.70% with episode-level returns versus 61.40% with step-level returns under identity return normalization, and 36.50% versus 58.20% under group-relative normalization. The authors caution that the annotation-coverage metric measures recovery of reference annotations under this protocol and does not by itself establish biological correctness or complete evidence grounding.

**Background**: Protein annotation agents are LLM-based systems that must select appropriate bioinformatics tools, interpret their outputs, and combine the resulting evidence into a final answer; most existing systems rely on frontier-scale models. REINFORCE is a classic policy-gradient reinforcement learning algorithm that directly optimizes the probability of actions that maximize expected cumulative reward. Credit assignment is the problem of determining which actions in a multi-step trajectory deserve credit for an eventual outcome, and step-level credit assignment has become an active research direction for training LLM agents on long tool-use or reasoning trajectories.

## [StateWise: Teaching LLMs to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33766) ⭐️ 7.0/10

StateWise introduces a self-improving fine-tuning method that trains a single LLM to maintain its own typed, revisable constraint state—including tombstones for revoked constraints—and adds a preference stage on self-generated relapse contrasts to reduce constraint relapse. On two backbones with held-out constraint families and unseen phrasings, it cuts relapse by 8–22 points relative to supervised self-training and lifts conversation success by 8–19 points over the backbone. Multi-turn instruction following is a critical failure mode for conversational assistants, where active constraints are forgotten and withdrawn ones are re-enacted. StateWise shows that a single model can learn to track and obey evolving constraints without external inference-time scaffolding, potentially simplifying deployment and improving reliability for real-world dialogue systems. The method fine-tunes on two skills—summarizing dialogue into constraint state and responding conditioned on that state—then self-trains on its own trajectories, keeping only turns that pass an exact round-trip check against compiled ground-truth states. Surprisingly, supervised variants roughly double relapse on Llama-3.1-8B, motivating a preference stage where rejected responses enact revoked rules; the paper also characterizes costs on general instruction-following benchmarks and studies weight interpolation as mitigation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Instruction-tuned LLMs often fail in multi-turn dialogue when users add, amend, or withdraw constraints over time: active constraints stop being honored (persistence failure) and withdrawn constraints keep being enacted (relapse). Existing repairs typically rely on an external ledger that re-injects a compiled specification every turn, adding inference-time scaffolding. StateWise instead teaches the model to maintain its own internal constraint state, using executable checkers to measure persistence and relapse and compiling ground-truth states for free.

## [CFL-aware edge design improves graph neural solvers for hyperbolic PDEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33769) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proposes making the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition an explicit edge-local signal in graph neural networks (GNNs) to better model hyperbolic PDEs. By varying only the form of edge information, the study finds that CFL conditioning reduces final-step error by 10.4–14.4% when the edge representation already separates direction from spatial scale, with the benefit growing for larger time steps. This work addresses a known stability issue in GNN-based PDE solvers—shock smearing and oscillations when extrapolating to larger time steps—by providing a specific design principle for edge features. It could impact scientific machine learning by enabling more robust and efficient simulation of transport phenomena, benefiting researchers and engineers working on fluid dynamics, wave propagation, and other hyperbolic systems. The study holds the GNN architecture fixed and varies only the edge information from raw edge form to forms that progressively expose direction, length, and wave speed. Appending CFL directly to a raw edge form yields almost no benefit; the improvement arises from suppressing oscillations near shocks rather than smearing the solution, and feature count is not the limiting factor.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) transport information at finite speed along characteristics and often produce shocks and discontinuities that are challenging to capture numerically. The Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition is a necessary stability criterion for numerical solutions of hyperbolic PDEs, relating the time step to the spatial grid size and wave speed. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as learned update rules for PDE solving, but standard neighbor aggregation does not explicitly encode how far information must travel along each edge.

## [TriageRAG: Failure-Aware Self-Training for Domain-Adapting RAG Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33776) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TriageRAG introduces a failure-aware self-training method that probes a student LLM on self-generated QA pairs both with and without retrieved context, triaging each example into one of four categories (known, solved, context-failure, retrieval-failure) and routing it to a tailored training signal. Experiments on 11 datasets across three domains with Qwen3-4B and on CS-Bench with Qwen3-8B show it outperforms a budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2–6.4 points and uniquely recovers closed-book performance when retrieval hurts the base model. This work addresses a key limitation of existing self-training approaches like SimRAG, which treat all retained examples identically and never diagnose whether failures stem from the reader or the retriever. By providing a label-free diagnostic of where the domain gap lies, TriageRAG could help practitioners build more robust RAG systems for specialized domains such as medicine, where unlabeled corpora are common but labeled data is scarce. The triage process is cheap and repeated every round, so the training mixture adapts to the student's evolving behavior, and the triage histogram serves as a diagnostic tool. An ablation reveals the mechanism: round-trip filtering removes all training contexts lacking evidence, causing a reader that never sees such contexts to over-trust noisy retrieval.

**Background**: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models by retrieving relevant evidence from an external knowledge base before generating an answer, improving reliability on knowledge-intensive tasks. Self-training methods like SimRAG adapt a general-purpose RAG system to a specialized domain by having the LLM generate its own question-answer pairs from domain passages and fine-tuning on pairs that pass a round-trip consistency filter. However, these methods do not distinguish between examples the model already knows, examples it can solve with retrieved context, and examples where it fails due to the reader or the retriever.

ProMo3D probes frozen 3D foundation model tokens and finds that static-dynamic separation is decodable from their representations, with motion cues concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. The data efficiency and zero-shot transfer to DAVIS, SegTrackv2, and FBMS-59 could make dense motion segmentation more accessible for 3D/4D vision research. The method is evaluated on three representative backbones, with rank-restricted and spectral analyses on π³X showing that recovered motion cues lie in a low-dimensional subspace. PMD outperforms training-free heuristics and approaches heavier supervised and self-supervised methods, though it is an arXiv preprint without community discussion.

## [LSTM memory advantage in XLand-MiniGrid is mostly evaluation noise and time-step confound](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33816) ⭐️ 7.0/10

An audit of an LSTM-vs-MLP comparison on a partially observable XLand-MiniGrid task finds that about ten paired seeds are needed to detect a 10-point gap in final success, and that the binary 'task acquired' metric is 76% evaluation noise, requiring about a hundred seeds for the same gap. On a sealed panel of new maps, a memory-free MLP of the LSTM's size given the time step comes within 3.3 points of the LSTM, and a linear probe reads the time step from the trained LSTM's state. This is a cautionary result for reinforcement learning benchmarking: a seemingly clear memory advantage can largely dissolve once evaluation noise and time-step information are separated out. It suggests that memory-free baselines should be given the time step, and that common binary learning-curve summaries may be far noisier than assumed. The study uses 60 runs each re-evaluated three times to decompose training seed, map, and evaluation randomness, and tests on a sealed panel of new maps opened only once. Even an MLP a quarter of the LSTM's size, and an LSTM with its state erased at every step, come within about 5 points when given the time step, and the MLP gains no measurable benefit from width without it.

## [Accumulation-Aware Training Makes DNNs Robust to Voltage Scaling Errors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33824) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces an accumulation-aware training method that combines mixed-precision quantization and unstructured pruning to make DNNs resilient to voltage scaling induced errors in systolic array accumulators. Evaluated on a 2nm technology node, the co-optimized post-layout architecture achieves 39% energy and 23% energy-delay product gains at low voltage while keeping accuracy degradation within 1%. This hardware-software co-design approach addresses the energy-reliability trade-off in DNN accelerators, enabling aggressive voltage scaling without sacrificing accuracy. It could significantly reduce power consumption in next-generation AI chips, impacting both hardware designers and ML practitioners deploying models on edge and data-center systems. The method constrains weight distributions to avoid activating sensitized high-rank carry chains in the accumulator, complemented by selective MSB-masking, fine-grained clock-gating, and layer-wise dynamic frequency scaling based on numerical sensitivity. The evaluation is on a deep-scaled 2nm node, but real-silicon validation and generalization to other accelerator architectures remain unaddressed.

## [Intervention-Certified Amplification: A Validity Gate for σ-Weighted Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33882) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Intervention-Certified Amplification (ICA), a method that gates σ-weighted SFT/RL hybrid post-training with paired-rollout target evidence to prevent the amplification of unintended behaviors. It demonstrates that a hybrid model (DIAA) emits unexecuted Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) on 29% of MATH-500 prompts, three times more than vanilla GRPO, and shows that ICA reduces TIR to 13.8% (frozen) and 11.2% (online) while improving accuracy from 47.5% to 48.7% and 49.3%, respectively. This work highlights a safety risk in hybrid post-training: training-side signals can inadvertently amplify pretrained behaviors that are unhelpful or even harmful for the target task. The proposed ICA gate offers a practical mechanism to validate and correct such amplification, which is important for the reliable deployment of RL-enhanced LLMs in reasoning-intensive applications. The paper quantifies that suppressing TIR recovers 10.6 percentage points of accuracy, and that a student trained on a 0%-TIR teacher anchor still emits TIR at 45.8%, underscoring the persistence of the behavior. ICA halves residual drag and transfers to held-out GSM8K without retuning, but the approach requires paired rollouts and may add computational overhead.

## [Counterfactual Test-Time Augmentation Removes Shortcuts in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33904) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proposes counterfactual test-time augmentation (CTTA), a family of methods that generate counterfactual edits to change shortcut values and average the LLM's predictions across edits. The authors prove that the optimal shortcut-invariant predictor belongs to this family and introduce Select-CTTA, which selects among CTTA methods using tests for assumption violations. Shortcut learning causes LLMs to rely on spurious correlations that fail under distribution shift, and existing fixes require training data, weight access, and heavy computation. CTTA works purely at test time, making robustness improvements accessible even when models are closed-source or training resources are unavailable. The optimal CTTA weights depend on the training distribution and are generally not identifiable from the trained model and unlabeled test data, but the paper presents assumptions under which they can be derived from token probabilities and proposes tests to detect violations. Empirically, Select-CTTA outperforms test-time baselines and approaches the performance of models fine-tuned on shortcut-balanced data.

The paper proposes Hierarchical Cooperative GFlowNets (HCG), a method that dynamically partitions the search space and coordinates multiple GFlowNets to avoid collapse onto high-reward regions and improve exploration. It introduces a shared classifier to coordinate the hierarchy and derives a normalizer-weighted aggregation rule for the ensemble. This approach addresses a key limitation of GFlowNets—mode collapse—by enabling broader exploration, which is crucial for applications like scientific discovery and combinatorial optimization. It provides a theoretical characterization and could inspire further research on ensemble methods for generative models. HCG imposes an ordering where the highest-ranked model explores the entire space while lower-ranked models are pushed toward uncovered regions, and the shared classifier partitions the space without hand-crafted boundaries. The normalizer-weighted aggregation rule is proven to recover the target reward-proportional distribution under stated assumptions, and experiments show improved mode coverage across multimodal distributions, sequence generation, combinatorial optimization, and biological sequence design.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are generative models that sample objects proportionally to a reward function, promoting diversity in generated samples. However, they can suffer from mode collapse, where the model concentrates on a few high-reward regions, leaving much of the space unexplored. HCG builds on this by coordinating multiple GFlowNets hierarchically to cover more modes.

## [ST-OPSD uses activation steering to fix reference hallucination in self-distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34005) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Steered-Teacher OPSD (ST-OPSD), an activation-steering method that extracts two directions from model-generated reasoning trajectories and applies them to the teacher's hidden states during distillation target computation. This suppresses reference-invoking behavior and encourages reconsideration with marker-family calibration, while the student learns from the resulting teacher distributions without being steered. This work addresses two specific failure modes—reference hallucination and reconsideration suppression—that undermine independent reasoning in thinking models trained via on-policy self-distillation. By restoring these behaviors to base-model levels and improving accuracy on AIME and HMMT, it offers a targeted fix that could make OPSD more reliable for reasoning model training. ST-OPSD extracts steering directions from model-generated reasoning trajectories and applies them only to the teacher's hidden states during target computation, leaving the student unsteered. Experiments on AIME and HMMT show improved accuracy over vanilla OPSD and other interventions, with reconsideration and reference-hallucination rates restored to base-model levels.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student model on its own reasoning trajectories using token-level supervision from a reference-conditioned teacher initialized from the same model. Activation steering is a technique that modifies a model's hidden states at inference time by injecting directional vectors to control its behavior. Reference hallucination refers to a model citing an unavailable reference to justify reasoning steps, while reconsideration suppression means the teacher discourages verification and revision at uncertain steps.

## [DeepSciReasoner predicts scientific spectra with physical constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34021) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced DeepSciReasoner, a general framework that predicts structured scientific spectra—such as electronic density of states (eDOS), phonon density of states (phDOS), XANES, and Raman spectra—by combining structure-aware decoding with constraint-preserving physical reasoning. Evaluated across these four spectrum types, the method substantially improves prediction accuracy while maintaining physical consistency. Accurate spectrum prediction is central to materials discovery, yet existing methods treat spectra as unconstrained sequences and fail to enforce hard physical laws such as conservation and characteristic spectral geometry. By providing a reusable blueprint for constraint-aware prediction, DeepSciReasoner could improve the reliability of machine-learning-driven materials screening. The framework is evaluated on eDOS, phDOS, XANES, and Raman spectra, using eDOS as the prototypical example, and it aims to capture rich spectral structure while respecting underlying physics. The abstract does not report specific accuracy metrics or benchmark comparisons, so the magnitude of improvement remains to be seen in the full paper.

## [KEEL framework evolves agent skills and lessons via verifier evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34043) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced KEEL (Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons), an agent-agnostic framework that uses verifier evidence to turn successful behaviors into reusable skills and failures into corrective lessons. On the SkillFlow benchmark, KEEL improves task success by 4.2 to 21.7 percentage points over the no-knowledge baseline, compared with gains of 2.4 to 9.6 points from SkillFlow's default method. This work addresses a key reliability problem in continual agent learning: automatically collected skills and memories can propagate errors and corrupt useful knowledge. By showing that validating and evolving knowledge matters more than simply accumulating experience, KEEL offers a principled mechanism that could improve how autonomous agents retain and improve performance across related tasks. As new evidence accumulates, individual skill claims can be supported, contradicted, replaced, or retired, and ablations show that skills and lessons are complementary. The framework is agent-agnostic, and code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/KEEL-TTCL26.

## [Sign Law Links Sampler Mismatch to Entropy Drift in RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34044) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proves that in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), sampler mismatch—where rollouts are drawn with top-k/top-p truncation or at a temperature the learner does not apply—causes a predictable sign of entropy drift depending on the sampler's likelihood ratio. Specifically, positive advantage shifts sharpen the policy under any sampler whose likelihood ratio to the policy increases with token probability (including top-k, top-p, min-p, and temperatures below one), and flatten it under flatter samplers. This result explains why seemingly neutral implementation choices, such as masking over-length responses or counting them as failures, can have opposite effects on policy entropy, which is critical for stable RLVR training. It offers a theoretical foundation for diagnosing and correcting entropy collapse or explosion in large language model reasoning training, affecting researchers and practitioners using group-based RL methods like GRPO. The paper shows that in group-based RLVR with token-level losses, the baseline-controlled part of entropy drift is set by the token-weighted net advantage, which masking and failing over-length responses can push to opposite signs; the remainder is a covariance between advantages and the sampler's sharpness gap that can feed back over long horizons. Experiments on a 2B model confirm the entropy slope is linear in shifts of the net advantage under truncated sampling but flat under exact sampling, and token-level importance ratios leave 98% of the drift; on a 9B reasoning model, zeroing the net advantage or renormalizing the learner gains 8.2 and 8.8 points over the uncorrected rule.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models using automatically checkable rewards, often on tasks like math and coding, and has gained attention through methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) used in DeepSeek-R1. In RLVR, rollouts are typically generated by an inference engine that may use truncation sampling (top-k, top-p, min-p) or temperature scaling, while the learner computes probabilities without such modifications, creating a mismatch. Entropy of the policy is a key quantity: too low entropy leads to collapse and lost exploration, while too high entropy causes instability. This paper provides a theoretical law for how sampler mismatch drives entropy in a predictable direction.

## [T2D: Pruning Target Models to Build Better Draft Models for Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34103) ⭐️ 7.0/10

T2D introduces a framework that constructs draft models directly from the target model using latency-aware structured pruning and knowledge distillation, jointly optimizing for distributional alignment and inference latency. Experiments show it can prune up to 92% of the target model while outperforming competitive baselines, and the resulting draft models can be plugged into other speculative decoding methods for further gains. Speculative decoding is a key technique for accelerating LLM inference, but its effectiveness hinges on balancing draft model quality and speed. T2D's joint optimization approach addresses this trade-off more systematically than prior methods that rely on independently pretrained small models or manual architecture choices, potentially making speculative decoding more practical for deployment. The method formulates draft model design as an optimization problem that minimizes both measured inference latency and cross-entropy loss on the target model's responses. It uses structured pruning (removing entire structures like layers or channels) combined with knowledge distillation, and the pruned models can serve as plug-and-play components for other token-alignment or distillation techniques.

**Background**: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive text generation by using a smaller draft model to propose multiple tokens ahead, which the larger target model then verifies in parallel, accepting tokens that match its own predictions. The speedup depends on how well the draft model's distribution aligns with the target model and how fast the draft model runs. Structured pruning removes entire neurons, channels, or layers from a neural network to reduce computation, while knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model.

HumanoidNDM introduces an online fine-tuning framework that uses a real-world-trained neural dynamics model to bridge the training-deployment gap in humanoid motion tracking. ## [DPR: Prune-and-Reconstruct for Memory-Efficient GNN Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34140) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DPR introduces a double-layer sparsification method that first prunes a graph to a compact core for efficient GNN training, then reconstructs pruned nodes with a sparse structure-aware decoder at inference. On a 30%-budget model, it trains in 1,450 MiB peak memory on a single 6 GB GPU and recovers 96.9% of its dense-reconstruction reference, beating the DSpar baseline by +1.36 pp at 50.1% lower peak training memory. This work reframes pruning from an irreversible accuracy tax into a safe training accelerator, enabling all-node inference on million-node graphs within VRAM limits. It could significantly benefit memory-constrained graph learning applications, such as production-scale recommendation or network analysis, where full-graph GNNs were previously infeasible. The deployed 30%-budget model pays a measured 2.64 pp accuracy tax versus a full-batch no-prune encoder for a 2.8x smaller training footprint, and all-node serving runs 46x faster than sampling-based GraphSAGE at a cost of about 5.4 pp test accuracy. The framework scales to a 2.45M-node production graph at 6,285 MiB peak training memory, while extended variants and the 41.8%-budget M4 point are reported separately and not directly compared with original-node baselines.

**Background**: Graph neural networks (GNNs) on million-node graphs often hit a memory wall before a compute wall, because storing node features and intermediate embeddings for all nodes can exceed GPU VRAM. Common remedies include mini-batch neighbor sampling, which can slow inference and lose accuracy, and graph pruning (e.g., edge sparsification like DSpar), which reduces memory but typically degrades accuracy permanently. DPR combines node pruning with a learned decoder that reconstructs pruned nodes from the compact core, aiming to recover accuracy while keeping the memory savings.

## [ECHO: Entropy-Based Closed-Loop Control to Prevent Catastrophic Forgetting in LLM Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34182) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces ECHO (Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization), a closed-loop control framework that uses output entropy as a real-time proxy for forgetting risk during supervised fine-tuning of LLMs. By decomposing KL divergence, the authors identify output entropy as a dominant observable component and employ a proportional controller to dynamically adjust replay data weights, avoiding expensive reference-model inference. Catastrophic forgetting is a major obstacle in continual learning and fine-tuning of LLMs, and ECHO offers a computationally efficient solution that balances plasticity and stability without requiring a reference model. Its empirical validation across 0.6B to 9B parameter models suggests it could be widely adopted for robust fine-tuning in real-world applications. ECHO uses deviations from the pre-trained entropic equilibrium as an error signal in a proportional control law to modulate replay gradient weights. Experiments show it lies on or extends the observed plasticity-stability frontier and maintains robustness across varying data mixing ratios.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when a model fine-tuned on new tasks loses previously learned knowledge. KL divergence measures the difference between probability distributions and is often used to quantify forgetting, but computing it requires inference on a reference model. Entropy, a measure of uncertainty in model outputs, can serve as a cheaper proxy for KL divergence under certain decompositions.

Researchers introduce BAC-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on repairing broken access control (BAC) vulnerabilities, comprising 46 real-world vulnerabilities from six web applications across four programming languages. They also propose a four-dimensional repair-strategy framework (Position, Coverage, Mechanism, Content) and find that base LLMs repair 37.68% of vulnerabilities on average, rising to 66.03% with minimal scaffolds and up to 75.36% for the best model. Broken access control is ranked as the top web application security risk by OWASP, yet automated repair for this logic-based vulnerability class has been largely unexplored. BAC-Bench provides the first standardized way to measure LLM capabilities in this domain, which could accelerate practical adoption of LLM-based security patching and spur further research. Each vulnerability in BAC-Bench comes with a sandboxed runtime environment, a proof-of-concept (PoC) validation program, and a functional test program. Notably, some LLM-generated patches outperformed official patches, and one incidentally fixed a zero-day vulnerability that had been dormant for three years.

## [SHIFT-Jev: Certified Abstention and Gain-Gated Adaptation for LLM Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34329) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SHIFT-Jev introduces a framework that monitors LLM-based decision models for distribution shift, certifies abstention thresholds via Learn-then-Test, and only accepts continual updates when a held-out expected-gain gate shows significant improvement without regressing on earlier regimes. On a ten-environment benchmark with Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-4B, and Phi-4-mini, fine-tuning with KL anchors and temperature scaling reduced calibration error under shift from 0.289 to 0.087. LLMs are increasingly deployed as decision models, but their reliability degrades under domain, label-prior, and candidate-set shifts; SHIFT-Jev provides a principled pipeline that combines statistical risk control with drift detection and conservative adaptation, which could make such deployments safer and more trustworthy. The strong calibration gains and the ability to detect class-prior shifts that confidence- and embedding-based detectors miss are particularly relevant for high-stakes applications. At a target risk of 10%, a learned uncertainty score with a certified threshold exceeds the target in only 3 to 5 of 27 environment-seed tests, compared to 5 to 15 for a max-probability score and 9 to 14 for conformal prediction sets; a chi-squared test on predicted labels detects 95–99% of class-prior shifts. In continual adaptation, SHIFT-Jev reaches 70.5% accuracy on Qwen3-0.6B, beating replay, LwF, EWC, and fine-tuning baselines in every seed, but on Qwen3-4B its conservative gate leaves it 0.4 to 1.4 points behind them.

**Background**: Distribution shift occurs when the data a model encounters at deployment differs from its training distribution, which can severely degrade the reliability of LLM-based decision models. Learn-then-Test (LTT) is a framework for calibrating predictive models to satisfy finite-sample statistical guarantees, such as risk control, without retraining. Temperature scaling is a post-processing calibration method that adjusts a single scalar to improve probability calibration, and KL anchoring regularizes fine-tuning to prevent catastrophic forgetting by penalizing divergence from a reference model.

The method targets neurons enriched in redundant reasoning by contrasting activations on long and short correct solutions, and it augments preference-based CoT compression with training signals from problems the pruned model always or never solves. Evaluated on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B at 20% pruning, it achieves 8–22% fewer thinking tokens on four math benchmarks with accuracy within 0.5 points compared to RAC pruning followed by the same compression.

## [Xing USP: A Cross-Family Semantic Contract for Structured Parsing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34343) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces USP, a cross-family semantic contract that unifies categories, fields, values, and instance associations across named-entity recognition, relation extraction, event extraction, and intent-slot parsing, paired with five diagnostic matching views. Using this contract, the authors normalize 61 datasets into a unified corpus and show that their fine-tuned Xing4.0-29B-Intent model achieves 57.70 task-balanced Field-Value Micro-F1, ranking first on all five views. Current evaluation of structured semantic parsing typically only checks category accuracy, overlooking value recovery and instance-level associations, so systems can appear correct while binding arguments to wrong instances. USP provides a shared representation and diagnostic protocol that make structural agreement measurable and comparable, potentially raising evaluation standards across extraction and intent-slot tasks. The five diagnostic views—category agreement, field recognition, field-value pairing, instance-bound assignment, and complete-instance recovery—ask distinct questions about the same output. The margin of Xing4.0-29B-Intent over the strongest alternative widens from 2.93 points for category matching to 20.73 points for complete-instance matching, showing that category agreement alone understates structural deficits.

Researchers built a benchmark of 40 protected skills across eight open- and closed-source science-agent platforms and found that all eight (100%) leak at least one skill, with four reaching 100% attack success under a single direct request. ## [Tail Calibration Predicts Finite-Budget Reward Hacking in Best-of-N Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34375) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.34375) proves that Best-of-N (BoN) selection depends on proxy scores only through their ranks, and that BoN can decline only when the calibration curve's tail turns downward, with the budget for decline determined by the error tail behavior. The authors derive a taxonomy under a bounded additive model: Gaussian errors keep improving, Laplace errors plateau, and heavy-tailed errors revert to the prior mean, and they validate this with synthetic phase maps and real candidate pools. This work provides a principled audit for reward hacking in inference-time scaling, showing that tail calibration can identify which budgets are at risk without being affected by monotone rescaling of reward scores. It is valuable for researchers and practitioners in LLM alignment and inference who rely on BoN selection with learned reward models. The analysis shows that BoN value equals a Beta-weighted integral of conditional true reward over within-prompt score quantiles, and a held-out tail calibration statistic reliably predicts where a cross-fitted budget cap helps, performing about as well as rank accuracy and competitive with a Soft-BoN baseline. On real candidate pools across several verifiable domains, base policies, and learned reward models, tail failures are rare and all occur in code generation.

## [Causal Structure Boosts Forward Model Safety in Synthetic Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34385) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper compares an Action-Conditioned Latent Structural Causal Model (AC-LSCM) against three unstructured forward models on seven random graphs with 10 or 20 variables, finding that AC-LSCM exactly recovers the true graph on all 10-variable graphs and achieves lower three-step prediction error in all 396 paired comparisons. The paper also withdraws an earlier claim of a 36x safety improvement, correcting it to a more modest reduction in safety violations relative to an oracle. This work provides rigorous empirical evidence that incorporating causal structure—specifically, using observed variables as factors—can improve an agent's ability to foresee multi-step action outcomes and avoid unsafe actions, which is directly relevant to AI safety and safe planning. It also highlights that the choice of factors matters more than explicit do-operators or counterfactual data, offering practical guidance for designing forward models in safety-critical applications. AC-LSCM uses per-factor mechanisms over a learned sparse graph with actions as do-interventions; when its factors are the observed variables, it reduces excess safety violations to 0.25 of the no-model level on 10-variable graphs (best baseline 0.31) and 0.41 on 20-variable graphs (0.53), with the largest margin for two-variable actions never seen in training. However, with learned latent factors the same model performs worse than baselines, and every planner remains far from the oracle.

Evaluations across speech, music, and sound show improved content and spatial quality, acoustic fidelity during editing, and better preservation of unedited sources compared to baselines.

A new arXiv paper (2610.34490) proposes a joint proof framework that integrates candidate answer selection, answer supplementation, and formal proof generation into a single call for Lean 4 statements. The core is a trained prover that selects given answers or proposes new ones and generates a proof for at least one answer in a single call; generated proofs can also be reused to detect faithfulness errors, since two distinct provable answers under the same formal statement indicate the statement does not faithfully preserve the original problem semantics. ## [Proactive memory recall in LLM assistants is a multiple-testing problem, scaling law shows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34507) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.34507) shows that proactive memory recall in long-lived assistants is a multiple-testing problem whose false-alarm rate grows with memory store size N. On streaming replays of LongMemEval and LoCoMo, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at N=8 reaches 87-100% at N=2048, and the authors derive a scaling law that predicts hit-rate decay as a power of N, matching a per-N oracle threshold within one percentage point. This work gives a theoretical explanation for why proactive memory recall degrades as assistants accumulate more memories, affecting the design of long-lived AI assistants and memory systems. It provides actionable guidance, such as thresholds that grow like ln N and sqrt(ln N) for lexical and semantic channels, and a label-free conformal gate that maintains false alarms near 5%. The paper proves that a gate with false-alarm rate alpha operates at a per-item false-positive rate of about -ln(1-alpha)/N, pinning hit rate to the far left of the single-comparison ROC curve and causing power-law decay under regular variation. A cue-swap conformal gate compares the current cue with the user's other cues on the same store, needs no labels, and has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability; three annotators (Fleiss' kappa=0.63) found about nine in ten false alarms are genuine interruptions.

Multiple-testing correction methods like false discovery rate (FDR) control are standard in statistics but have not been widely applied to memory recall in LLM agents.

## [TRIAGE: Hybrid KV Reuse and Token Pruning Speeds Up VLA Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34519) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TRIAGE introduces a training-free method that, for each skipped visual token in a vision-language-action model, decides whether to reuse its cached KV state or prune it based on a token-level 'drift' diagnostic. On LIBERO and SimplerEnv benchmarks, it stays within 3 percentage points of full recomputation while cutting prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%. Real-time robot control on onboard embedded hardware is bottlenecked by the prefill latency of processing hundreds of visual tokens per step, and TRIAGE's per-token hybrid approach outperforms prune-only or reuse-only accelerators, making VLA models more practical for mobile manipulators and humanoids. The diagnostic shows that reusing tokens below a drift threshold is no worse than pruning, but beyond it reuse yields up to 4.4x the action error of pruning; TRIAGE recomputes a fixed budget of important tokens with invalid caches, reuses valid ones, and prunes the rest, with the budget directly setting prefill latency. With only 7% of visual tokens recomputed, it beats the strongest baseline by 24.4 percentage points on LIBERO-Object.

## [SentryBench: Cost-Sensitive Benchmark for Adversarial Robustness of Tool-Using LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34535) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SentryBench introduces a two-sided, cost-sensitive benchmark that jointly measures attack success, over-refusal, and over-reaction for tool-using LLM agents in public-safety scenarios, grounded in real emergency-call transcripts and injection/jailbreak payloads. Across 840 scored episodes with three frontier models and three defenses, the authors show that naive 'refuse-more' caution drives over-refusal to 100% on two of three models while barely reducing attack success, whereas a targeted trust-gating wrapper achieves the lowest harm on every model. This work challenges the common assumption that refusing is the safe default for agents wired to consequential tools like dispatching responders or sending public alerts, where a missed emergency is as harmful as a false alarm. It offers a deployment-oriented evaluation framework that could reshape how public-safety and other high-stakes agent systems are benchmarked and defended. The paper formalizes deployment harm as an asymmetric cost functional and proves that naive caution is harm-dominated whenever it refuses more genuine emergencies than the attack harm it averts, while a targeted trust gate adds zero over-refusal on clean input. It also notes that provider content filters silently perform part of the defending and must be reported separately.

RIDE-Splat introduces a two-pass pipeline that separates camera-attached windshield reflections from world-consistent scene content to enable reflection-free 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction from in-the-wild driving video. RIDE-Splat assigns world-consistent transmission through the windshield to a 3DGS scene and the dominant camera-attached reflection to one shared, signed RGB image; it first learns 3D geometry and the signed reflection image (representing added radiance and transmission attenuation), then fits a clean 3DGS model using reflection-removed training images. At inference, the reflection image is discarded, preserving the standard 3DGS rendering path, and the method achieves the highest metrics in 38 out of 42 per-scene comparisons.

The paper introduces OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type, along with the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies, the authors find that neither consistently adapts motion to obstacle safety semantics, even with explicit safety prompts. This work exposes a concrete gap in semantic-to-motion grounding: policies can recognize obstacle safety relevance but fail to translate that recognition into appropriately safe continuous motion. The benchmark and metric provide a targeted evaluation tool for robotics and embodied AI safety research, highlighting the need for models that convert semantic caution into physical behavior. The benchmark uses spatially matched scenario sets that isolate obstacle type as the only variable, and SSI quantifies whether clearance, distance-dependent speed, and smoothness follow a caution ordering. For VLM-based policies that recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, inserting an explicit parameter-inference step between recognition and program generation improves adaptation.

## [Certify uses Horn-closure certificates to decide evidence sufficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34684) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Certify, a method that decomposes a query into a requirement hypergraph, searches per requirement, and applies Horn closure over entity-checked links to produce a certificate of minimal sufficient passages or an abstention naming open requirements. Pooled over three corpora with unanswerable twins, Certify decides significantly more accurately than search agents, graph retrieval, and sufficiency judges, and its certificate-based answers are 80% correct versus 57% from all retrieved passages. This work replaces holistic model judgement of evidence sufficiency with a structural, formally sound decision procedure, which could reduce confident but unsupported answers in search-augmented and RAG systems. It matters for anyone building retrieval-augmented LLM pipelines that must decide when to answer, search again, or abstain. Given correct retrieval, requirements, and links, the decision is sound and complete up to the entity check; over 21M Wikipedia passages, entity checks add 4 to 13 points of decision accuracy where gold evidence exists. The method matches a proprietary model's sufficiency label without an additional model call, though it is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

## [VLA-HWBench: Action Strategy, Not Model Size, Dominates Edge Latency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34717) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces VLA-HWBench, a benchmark of 18 open vision-language-action (VLA) models on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395 with a seven-stage inference breakdown. It finds that action-generation strategy dominates latency more than model size, with latency varying by 82x on Jetson and 157x on AMD, while parameter count explains at most 15% of latency variance. This counterintuitive finding suggests that robotics practitioners should prioritize action-generation design and inference software optimizations over simply shrinking models to achieve real-time closed-loop control on edge hardware. It provides actionable guidance for VLA deployment on robots, where latency directly constrains control responsiveness. Kernel fusion with 4-bit weights yields the largest speedup, making π0.5 and GR00T N1.7 2.6–2.9x faster than PyTorch with torch.compile, but this optimization exists only for these two models and only on Jetson. After optimization, memory bandwidth limits only stages processing few tokens (e.g., denoising), while software limits all other stages, and CPU preprocessing grows from 12% to 39% of the GR00T N1.7 call.

## [Coding agents' context cost should be measured by executed prefill, not prompt tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34763) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.34763) proposes a quality-constrained resource accounting protocol that splits executed prefill into logical prompt minus reused prefix and measures KV residency, time, and energy. On 450 localization cases from SWE-rebench V2, preloading ten retrieved blocks (Eager) and adding anchored history compaction (Compact) both pass a five-point non-inferiority gate; in a 900-cell study, Eager cuts model calls by 35.7% and the GPU-energy proxy by 33.2% versus on-demand search (Grep). This work shows that judging context policies by prompt tokens alone is misleading, because a shorter prompt can cost more if it rewrites cached history and forces re-prefill. For agent builders, the finding that deleting history can multiply physical work (uncached prefill up 608.5% in one experiment) has direct implications for how context management and prefix caching are designed and evaluated. Enabling prefix caching leaves Eager's prompt volume similar (+8.3%, with a 95% CI spanning zero) but cuts its uncached prefill by 67.7%; meanwhile, keeping only the last five observations (Mask-5) cuts prompt volume by 33.3% but loses 135.9k reusable tokens per task, raises uncached prefill by 608.5% and the energy proxy by 125.6%, and misses the quality gate. Compact adds no further savings beyond Eager in the 900-cell study.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Coding agents resend a growing context on every model call, and context policies are usually judged by the prompt tokens they save. However, executed work also depends on call count and prefix reuse: a caching runtime prefills only the tokens after the longest cached prefix, so a shorter prompt can cost more if it rewrites cached history. Prefix caching (KV-cache reuse) is a common inference optimization that avoids recomputing shared prompt prefixes, and context compaction lets long-horizon agents continue beyond their context windows but can erase state needed to finish a task.

## [Study finds silent prompt-caching mis-integrations in LLM agents, proposes CACHELINT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34817) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper presents the first empirical study of 120 prompt-caching-related pull requests from 10 popular open-source LLM agent systems, revealing both request-side misconfiguration and read-side usage miscount that mostly fail silently. The authors propose CACHELINT, a detector that uses CodeQL to locate caching invocation sites and checks preconditions against a dated provider capability oracle or an LLM guard, achieving 0.71 precision and 0.78 recall on the labeled set and 0.86 precision across 571 real-world projects. Prompt caching is a key lever for reducing inference cost and latency in production LLM systems, but mis-integrations that fail silently can quietly inflate bills without triggering runtime errors. The study's 21 developer confirmations and 18 upstream fixes, including one in Anthropic's official SDK, show the problem is real and that automated detection can meaningfully improve production reliability. CACHELINT models a mis-integration as an invocation site plus the preconditions required for correct caching, discharging each precondition either against a dated provider capability oracle or via an LLM guard check. The approach targets heterogeneous, continuously evolving provider-specific caching APIs, and the real-world scan of 571 agent projects found 32 mis-integrations with 0.86 precision.

**Background**: Prompt caching stores frequently unchanged parts of a prompt, such as system instructions or reference material, so the model does not reprocess those tokens on every call, cutting cost and latency. On providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, caching is typically a prefix match: a single changed byte before the cache marker invalidates everything after it, so correct integration depends on precise request construction and accurate accounting of cache reads. Because each provider exposes different APIs and caching semantics evolve over time, downstream agent developers can easily misconfigure caching in ways that produce no visible error.

## [SPARTA: Sparse Ternary LLM Accelerator for Long-Context Edge Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34824) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SPARTA is a new sparse ternary LLM accelerator that unifies ternary linear and attention datapaths and introduces an adaptive two-stage attention engine combining page-level Top-k selection and token-level Top-p pruning. It reduces KV-cache traffic by 4.1–4.8x over full attention and achieves 3.9x higher generation throughput and 8.3x higher energy efficiency than NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Long-context inference on edge devices is increasingly bottlenecked by KV-cache traffic, and SPARTA's unified datapath and adaptive attention directly target this bottleneck, potentially enabling more capable on-device LLM applications. Its significant gains over existing accelerators like FIGLUT, TeLLMe, and MCBP suggest a path toward more efficient edge AI hardware. SPARTA employs a phase-aware sparse dataflow that exploits heterogeneous sparsity across compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode, and maps ternary SpMM/SpMV and bit-serial attention onto shared processing elements to exploit zero-weight and zero-bit sparsity. The adaptive attention incurs task-dependent quality loss, and the reported gains versus AMD Ryzen 7 9700X are 5.0x throughput and 81.7x energy efficiency.

The paper introduces Streaming Recurrent Memory (SRM), a recurrent memory architecture that learns from a continuous stream of experience without storing raw data, using one-step backpropagation through time (BPTT). ## [AIPC: Evidence-Guided Agent Workflows for PyTorch Deployment on NPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34890) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AIPC (AI Porting & Conversion) is a new LLM-agent method that combines structured Skills with toolchain, runtime, and profiling evidence to diagnose and repair cross-layer issues when deploying PyTorch inference projects onto dedicated accelerators such as NPUs. Evaluated on Qualcomm QAIRT's on-device NPU path across vision, speech, LLM, and diffusion models, it achieved 6/7 successful Whisper-Small runs versus 0/6 for the control, and a 2.791x end-to-end speedup for YOLO-Worldv2 versus 1.599x for the control. Deploying PyTorch models to NPUs is notoriously difficult because it requires converting models into hardware-runtime artifacts and adapting to toolchain, quantization, and operator constraints, which creates cross-layer problems that LLM agents often fail to handle without domain knowledge. AIPC's evidence-guided approach shows that agents can automate this complex porting process with minimal human intervention, potentially lowering the barrier for deploying models on edge accelerators and reducing engineering effort. The method organizes model adaptation, artifact building, on-target execution, accuracy repair, and performance optimization into a single deployment flow, and under a pre-fixed deployment contract with skill, tool permissions, and check conditions, some runs achieved zero in-run human intervention (0-HITL). The authors also examine Qwen3.8-27B as a locally deployable model for driving the agent workflow, though the approach is evaluated only on Qualcomm's QAIRT NPU path and remains an arXiv preprint without community discussion.

## [Waypoint: Analytical GEMM Tiling Model for CPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34914) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present Waypoint, an analytical model that automatically selects the optimal GEMM tile size for a given CPU hardware and matrix shape by estimating performance across memory hierarchy, instruction-level parallelism, and multi-threading effects. They also introduce OPAM, a new CPU GEMM library built on Waypoint that matches state-of-the-art libraries and accelerates LLM inference by 1.36–1.98×. GEMM is the core computational kernel in deep learning and scientific computing, and tile size selection is critical for performance; an analytical model that avoids exhaustive empirical autotuning could simplify library development and portability across CPUs. The demonstrated LLM inference speedups show direct practical value for deploying models on CPU-only or CPU-heavy systems. Waypoint uses its performance estimates as a proxy to search the space of possible tile sizes and can also help hardware designers estimate realistic performance on experimental hardware optimizations. The reported 1.36–1.98× LLM inference speedups are on CPUs, and OPAM's performance is described as matching, rather than exceeding, state-of-the-art GEMM libraries.

**Background**: General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) is a fundamental linear algebra operation used throughout deep learning and high-performance computing. High-performance GEMM implementations partition the output matrix into tiles that fit into cache and registers, and the chosen tile dimensions strongly affect achieved performance. Traditionally, optimal tile sizes are found through empirical autotuning, which is time-consuming and hardware-specific; analytical models aim to predict good configurations without exhaustive benchmarking.

## [Coding agents' self-evolution often fails to reduce repeated work, study finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34938) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.34938) empirically studies "retro," a skill that asks a coding agent to review a completed session and propose changes to its harness. Running Claude Code on 30 SWE-bench Verified issues produced 125 proposals, of which 24 were implemented and 12 evaluated on later issues; only two changes eliminated the targeted repeated action, while four showed no reduction and some added work on unrelated issues. This is one of the first rigorous empirical looks at whether coding agents can meaningfully self-improve their own operating environment, a capability increasingly marketed as a path to more autonomous software engineering. The results suggest that generating and applying harness changes is not enough—agents need mechanisms to validate, revise, or remove changes that don't help, which has direct implications for how teams build self-evolving agent pipelines. Most of the 125 proposals referred to a specific event in the session, but 18 of 43 lint-related proposals recommended a general practice regardless of what had happened. Among the seven evaluations where sessions without the change actually encountered the targeted problem, two changes eliminated the targeted action, one reduced it, four showed no reduction, and some changes added work on unrelated issues.

## [Study Identifies Four Reasoning Patterns in AI Coding Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34943) ⭐️ 7.0/10

An empirical study of large reasoning models (LRMs) across four coding tasks identifies four general reasoning patterns: design-to-implementation for code generation, state tracing for execution reasoning, evidence-fix-recheck for debugging, and semantic mapping for translation. It further distinguishes positive patterns linked to valid traces and negative patterns linked to invalid traces, and demonstrates three applications: task identification, pattern-guided prompting, and pattern-aware early stopping. This work provides a structured characterization of how LRMs reason during coding, enabling inference-time control mechanisms such as early stopping that reduce token usage with only a modest drop in pass@1. It could inform the design of more efficient and reliable AI coding assistants and guide future model development. The study transforms reasoning traces into structured action sequences and mines recurring fragments using within-task support, cross-task contrasts, and valid-invalid support contrasts. The three applications generalize to previously unseen models, and negative pattern-aware early stopping substantially reduces API-reported token usage while causing only a modest decrease in pass@1.

## [Info-GRPO: Mutual Information Regularization for Long-Trace Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34949) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.34949) proposes Info-GRPO, an information-theoretic framework that replaces entropy regularization in GRPO training by cultivating mutual information between a latent prior and the reasoning trajectory. On AIME24, it improves Avg@8 over vanilla GRPO by 3.75%, 1.66%, 4.16%, and 4.17% across four backbones, and reaches the same majority-vote accuracy with 8× fewer samples. Policy collapse is a known and active problem when training long chain-of-thought reasoning models with GRPO, and entropy regularization's per-token bonus conflicts with the entropy decay needed for convergence. Info-GRPO offers a conceptually different way to maintain exploration across whole reasoning traces, which could make RL training of reasoning models more stable and sample-efficient. Instead of raising entropy everywhere, Info-GRPO augments prompts with latent seeds during training so the model explores diverse policies correlated with the prior, while seed-conditioned entropy is guided toward convergence. The approach is a single arXiv preprint without community discussion or independent validation yet, and code and models are promised to be publicly released.

**Background**: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is the reinforcement learning algorithm behind DeepSeek-R1 that trains LLMs by comparing completions within a group and normalizing advantages, avoiding a separate value model. As reasoning traces grow to thousands of tokens, GRPO training is prone to policy collapse, where the policy becomes overly deterministic and loses exploration. Entropy regularization is the standard remedy, adding a bonus to keep output distributions from collapsing, but in long-trace regimes its coefficient is hard to tune and it fights the entropy decay that convergence requires. Info-GRPO draws on mutual information between a latent variable and the trajectory it induces, a technique used in multi-agent RL to encourage diverse yet coordinated behaviors.

GUIFlow introduces a framework for full-pipeline incremental inference in multi-image GUI interaction, selectively updating computational states across steps to avoid redundant recomputation. These mechanisms enable cross-step reuse in visual encoding, prefill, and decoding without additional training, a separate draft model, or changes to model-visible inputs and action interface.

## [Self-Criticism Boosts LLM Red Teaming, Self-Proposal Hurts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34965) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.34965) disentangles the roles of criticism and proposal in LLM-driven automatic red teaming, finding that self-criticism by the target session improves attack success while self-proposal by the target is substantially less effective. The role-separated approach—target diagnoses failures, separate attacker proposes next attack—achieves 63.2% overall attack success rate on DTAP-BENCH across Telecom, Workflow, CRM, and Code domains. This work shows that effective automatic red teaming depends not only on model capability and search strategy but also on how execution context and adversarial responsibility are distributed across model sessions, offering a concrete design principle for AI safety researchers building attack-discovery loops. It could influence how security teams architect LLM-based red-teaming systems and how model providers think about sandbagging and refusal behaviors. Self-criticism is more effective because it is grounded in the target's live execution context—observations, constraints, and available reasoning—and removing reasoning reduces downstream attack success by 6%–17%. Self-proposal is weaker because awareness of the adversarial objective induces explicit refusal and non-refusal sandbagging, and the findings hold across direct misuse and indirect threat models and multiple agent frameworks.

## [SVD-Attention Diagnoses Redundant Attention Heads Without Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34971) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SVD-Attention is a post-hoc method that decomposes each attention head's query-key interaction matrix and scores singular modes by spectral magnitude and activation variance on a small calibration set, identifying which heads actually use their full rank budget. Across seven pretrained models and five task types, it finds task-dependent redundancy patterns: early-to-middle layers for sentiment, image classification, and generation, and late layers for dense prediction and extractive QA. This diagnostic offers a practical way to locate redundant attention heads without retraining, which can guide efficient inference and model compression. Its predictive power—truncating flagged layers costs at most 1.75 F1 versus up to 50 F1 elsewhere—suggests it could help practitioners target pruning more safely. The factorization is exact for retained modes and requires no finetuning, but SVD-Attention is an analysis tool rather than a compression method: acting on it reduces inference FLOPs by only 0.8–1.5% alone, or 8–11% when composed with weight pruning, with 0–4% change in task quality.

**Background**: Transformers spend much of their inference compute in self-attention, where each head computes query-key interactions. Singular value decomposition (SVD) is a linear algebra technique that factorizes a matrix into rotation, scaling, and rotation, revealing its dominant modes; SVD-Attention applies this per head to measure which singular directions are actually activated.

The transformer memorizes training data within 250 steps, but grokking onset (first step at which test accuracy reaches 95%) varies from 6,500 to 21,000 steps; networks that memorize without grokking compress far less. Capping the rank of the transformer's MLP input weights delays onset, and capping the rank of its embedding stops 15 of 20 runs from grokking, confirming that compression is not the cause.

## [CarbonRouter: Cache-Aware Carbon Routing for Multi-Turn LLM Services](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35230) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present CarbonRouter, an online framework that jointly selects the model, GPU type, and region for each query in multi-turn LLM web services to minimize carbon emissions while accounting for the cost of recomputing the KV cache when a session moves. In trace-driven experiments on two real-world conversation datasets with five LLMs, three GPU types, and four regions, CarbonRouter reduced CO2 emissions by 16.1% on average compared to FairCarbon, a state-of-the-art carbon-aware router, with savings rising to 23.1% for sessions longer than 30 turns. Existing carbon-aware LLM routers treat each query independently and ignore the stateful nature of conversations, so they may move a session to a cleaner region only to incur a large recomputation cost that outweighs the carbon savings. CarbonRouter addresses this gap by explicitly modeling KV cache locality, making carbon-aware routing practical for real multi-turn web services and contributing to sustainable AI systems. CarbonRouter introduces a cache-aware carbon cost model that charges history recomputation to every candidate deployment using cached-token counts from serving backends, and a lightweight gate that keeps a session on its cached deployment when it would likely move back at the next turn and rebuild its history again. The evaluation also shows improvements in predicted answer quality and estimated latency, though the work is simulation-based and relies on trace-driven experiments rather than production deployment.

Evaluated on a continuous stirred-tank reactor with unmodeled Haldane inhibition, Luong product toxicity, and secondary metabolite autocatalysis, the framework recovered ground-truth parameters with under 6% error without prior kinetic knowledge. The framework uses logarithmic decomposition to decouple multiplicative (inhibitory) and additive (regulatory) residual channels, and an Active Design of Experiments (DoE) controller triggers targeted perturbations when statistical degeneracy occurs to decorrelate competing hypotheses. The isolation-peeling algorithm mathematically decouples entangled rate laws across orthogonal operational regimes.

A new empirical study evaluated 42 trajectory-reduction configurations across 9,400 runs with two state-of-the-art agents on SWE-bench Verified, finding that deleting up to 100% of reasoning text from old turns can preserve overall effectiveness if the deletion is delayed rather than applied immediately. This work challenges the assumption that aggressive context reduction necessarily harms agent performance and provides practical guidance for building cost-efficient LLM-based software engineering agents, though it also reveals that token savings do not always translate to lower costs under caching-aware pricing.
