## [GenSfM: Joint 3D Reconstruction and Generation via Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35522) ⭐️ 7.0/10

GenSfM integrates image-based 3D reconstruction with a native 3D diffusion model by using a multi-modal diffusion transformer to jointly denoise shape and per-view pose latents under shared self-attention. On Toys4k and GSO with 4 uncalibrated views, it improves novel-view PSNR by 3.2–4.5 dB and reduces median Chamfer distance by 2.8–3.8× over a strong native-3D generation baseline, while recovering input-view poses over 96% Acc@5° without external pose estimation or known intrinsics. This work addresses the error cascading problem in naive concatenation of reconstruction and generation, enabling 3D objects that are both faithful to input images and plausible in unseen regions. It could benefit applications like AR/VR, robotics, and content creation where only a few uncalibrated views are available. The method uses a compact 3D-native UV-volume tokenization to keep the joint sequence small as views are added, and a pose-aware stage refines geometry and texture by sampling per-voxel image features at the recovered camera poses. It requires no post-hoc optimization or external pose-estimation backbone.

## [RAINFALL: LLM-based ranking function synthesis for loop termination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35523) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose RAINFALL, a neuro-symbolic framework that uses LLMs with symbolic verification feedback to automatically synthesize ranking functions for proving loop termination in C programs. On two public benchmarks of 358 terminating C programs, RAINFALL with MiniMax V2.7 synthesizes verifiable ranking functions for 323 programs (90.22%), outperforming all baselines and solving 12 more programs than PROTON 2.1, the winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination category. This work demonstrates that LLMs can be effectively integrated into formal verification workflows, potentially reducing the expertise required for termination proofs. The generate-verify-refine paradigm with symbolic feedback offers a generic approach that could extend to other liveness certificates and formal verification tasks. RAINFALL formulates ranking function synthesis as a code-completion task by inserting placeholders into the input program and constraining the LLM to fill four predefined slots per loop; a symbolic verifier checks the completed program, and its diagnostics are translated into natural-language feedback for iterative refinement. Combining RAINFALL with PROTON 2.1 raises the success rate to 96.65% (346/358 programs), and ablation studies confirm the contributions of placeholder contracts, few-shot examples, symbolic verification, and diagnostic feedback.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: A ranking function is a mathematical function that maps each program state to a value from a well-founded set, such that the value strictly decreases with each loop iteration, thereby proving termination. Constructing such functions manually is difficult and requires significant expertise, and automated synthesis is challenging because termination is undecidable in general. Neuro-symbolic approaches combine neural generation with symbolic reasoning to leverage the strengths of both, and the generate-verify-refine paradigm iteratively improves LLM outputs using feedback from a verifier.

## [JANUS: Automated Cross-Layer Defense Synthesis Against Deserialization Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35532) ⭐️ 7.0/10

JANUS, a red-blue adversarial framework, iteratively synthesizes and refines cross-layer defenses against web deserialization exploit variants in an offline environment. Evaluated on 16 vulnerability deployments across six Java and PHP applications, it reduced held-out attack success to 6.2% versus 18.8–55.0% for baselines, fully mitigating 13 of 16 deployments while preserving 98.4% of benign functionality tests at a 6.9% targeted P95 latency increase. Unsafe deserialization is a pervasive web security flaw where a single vulnerability can spawn many exploit variants that evade single-point defenses. JANUS automates the coordination of defenses across gateway, application, and system layers, potentially reducing the expert effort needed to harden real-world applications against evolving attacks. The framework uses a black-box attacker that probes policies using only externally observable feedback, and a defender that summarizes verified variants into security-relevant effects and uses counterfactual replay to distinguish complementary coverage from redundant enforcement. Each candidate policy is validated against accumulated exploits and benign workflows, though the evaluation is limited to Java and PHP applications and a single arXiv preprint.

A new arXiv paper introduces VELA, an executable benchmark of 44 web vulnerabilities across twelve application families, and evaluates three commercial AI agents on agent-facing interfaces. The study finds that 91% of vulnerabilities remain exploitable under the reference interface design, and that interface configuration shifts exploitability from 39% to 95%, far outweighing agent choice (at most 4.5 points). ## [OpTTA: Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation Improves World Model Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35636) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA), which augments the standard prediction loss with the planner's goal-reaching cost when adapting a world model at test time. Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching, and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success by 13.5 percentage points on average over a frozen model, compared with 6.9 points for the prediction-only baseline AdaJEPA. This work shows that prediction-only test-time adaptation can be insufficient for planning, because low prediction error does not guarantee that the model is accurate about goal-reaching actions. The optimistic, task-aware objective offers a simple way to improve closed-loop planning under distribution shift without extra environment interaction, which could benefit model-based reinforcement learning systems deployed in changing real-world conditions. OpTTA minimizes two terms over model parameters: the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner's goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, biasing adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal. Experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives, and use both CEM and gradient-based planners; when the encoder is also adapted, gains are 13.5 versus 7.5 points.

The sample complexity bound is 1/(μ_min ε^2 (1-γ)^3 max{1-γ,σ}) + t_mix/(μ_min (1-γ)) up to logarithmic factors, where μ_min is the minimum state-action occupancy probability, t_mix is the mixing time, and σ is the uncertainty level; the algorithm assumes access to a single trajectory of Markovian samples and the nominal transition kernel.

The framework generalizes existing child-protective instruments and is designed to be institution-agnostic.

## [Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution for Multi-Objective RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35733) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces objective-conflict coefficients to quantify how misalignment between objectives affects learning efficiency, derives near-optimal regret bounds for online settings, and proposes routed ensemble policy learning that maintains a small set of basis policies and dynamically routes trajectories to the policy with the highest potential reward. It also presents a kernel surrogate trajectory attribution algorithm that estimates how feedback from a set of trajectories influences policy learning on other trajectories, capturing nonlinear interactions such as synergy and antagonism. This work provides a theoretical framework for understanding how conflicting objectives degrade sample efficiency in multi-objective reinforcement learning, which is relevant to AI alignment (e.g., balancing helpfulness and honesty) and robotics (e.g., trading off speed and energy). The routed ensemble approach improves average performance by 4.3% over baselines on Meta-World and MO-Gymnasium, and kernel-based attribution yields a 27% reward improvement in trajectory selection, suggesting practical benefits for sample-efficient policy learning. The regret bounds are derived for online settings using the objective-conflict coefficients, and the kernel surrogate attribution improves correlation with leave-one-out analysis by 50% over existing baselines. The approach is evaluated across diverse environments and benchmarks, but the abstract does not specify the number of basis policies or the computational overhead of routing.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-objective reinforcement learning extends standard RL to environments with multiple, often conflicting reward signals, where the optimal policy can vary sharply with different objective weightings. Traditional per-preference policy learning is sample-inefficient because it requires learning a separate policy for each weighting. Ensemble methods maintain multiple policies to cover different trade-offs, and trajectory attribution aims to understand how individual trajectories contribute to learning, which can help select informative data.

## [dSpark: Schedule Distillation Speeds Up Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35804) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces dSpark, a schedule distillation framework that learns which tokens to commit first in diffusion language models (dLLMs) to reduce decoding rounds. On GSM8K, dSpark achieves 10.12× and 5.12× speedups over baselines on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, respectively, while maintaining superior task performance. This work addresses a key bottleneck in dLLM inference—the number of decoding rounds—by prioritizing tokens that make other positions easier to predict, potentially enabling faster and more efficient parallel generation. It could benefit researchers and practitioners focused on efficient LLM inference and acceleration. dSpark constructs unmasking schedules that reveal tokens whose commitment reduces uncertainty for other positions, then distills these schedules into the model with a KL-divergence regularizer to preserve generation quality. The method is evaluated on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, with code available on GitHub.

**Background**: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are iterative denoising models that generate text by progressively recovering corrupted token sequences, allowing parallel token generation unlike autoregressive models. However, they often require many decoding rounds to complete a response, which limits efficiency. Schedule distillation refers to training a model to follow a teacher's token commitment order, and KL divergence is a common measure of difference between probability distributions used here as a regularizer.

## [REVA: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection via LLM Contextual Probing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35829) ⭐️ 7.0/10

REVA is a new AI vulnerability detector that combines a pre-computed threat model, static analysis findings, and call-graph context into a single forward pass of an LLM, then uses a trained probe to read the model's internal representations. On the PrimeVul held-out test set with GLM-5.3-Flash, it achieves 60.0% accuracy in about one second per function, matching the agentic detector VulTriage (59.2%) while being over 250 times faster and less than a tenth as costly. As coding agents generate code faster than humans can review, real-time screening of every new function becomes critical, and REVA shows that much of the context gathered by slower agentic detectors is already encoded in an LLM's internal representations. This could enable practical, low-cost security tooling integrated directly into AI-assisted development pipelines. The probe is 14% to 17% more accurate than the LLM's own direct verdict on the same prompt, and across three open LLMs REVA is at least as accurate as VulTriage, about 10% more accurate on two of them. However, the work is an arXiv preprint without peer review, and results are limited to the PrimeVul benchmark and specific open models.

Recent LLM agents can find real vulnerabilities by reasoning over multiple tool calls and code exploration, but this takes minutes per verdict, too slow for real-time use. REVA bridges this gap by distilling the agent's contextual understanding into a single LLM forward pass and reading the model's hidden states with a trained probe, a technique known as contextual probing.

## [GPT-6-Astra as Robot Agent: Direct Control vs. Harness with Policies on EBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35832) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv report evaluates GPT-6-Astra, a frontier multimodal large language model, as the core of a robot-controlling agent on EBench, comparing direct waypoint control against a harness that can invoke post-trained VLA or WAM policies. The study finds that direct control is competitive overall and leads on short-horizon tasks with the least variation across generalization dimensions, while the harness-with-policy configuration raises overall success to the level of the strongest post-trained policies and substantially reduces token cost. This work provides one of the first systematic comparisons between using a frontier MLLM as a direct robot controller and using it as a high-level agent that orchestrates specialized VLA/WAM policies, offering a novel agent-harness framing for robot learning. The findings could inform the design of future robot agents that combine the generalization of large models with the precision of post-trained policies. Under direct control, the agent underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks, and the harness-with-policy setup remains below the per-task upper bound of standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. The evaluation uses the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol for both agent configurations and post-trained policies.

## [New Benchmark Exposes Harmful Memorization in LLM Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.02296) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes a code rewriting pipeline that creates semantically altered versions of coding tasks and introduces the Harmful Memorization Index (HMI) to measure when models fail to adapt, producing code overly similar to original solutions. Evaluations on MBPP+ and BigCodeBench show HMI does not scale monotonically with model size and that supervised fine-tuning can increase HMI on held-out tasks. This work addresses a critical gap in evaluating code LLMs: distinguishing benign code reuse from harmful memorization that masks brittleness under small semantic changes. It provides a practical diagnostic tool that complements standard accuracy metrics, with implications for model safety, training data contamination detection, and post-training method selection. HMI combines similarity to the original solution with performance degradation on rewritten tasks, but it does not establish whether the original task or solution appeared in training data. High-HMI failures concentrate in specific logic-edit types, especially constraint changes and data transformations, and PPO yields a more favorable accuracy-HMI trade-off than SFT across evaluated post-training settings.

This paper defines harmful memorization behaviorally as failure to adapt when task semantics change, and proposes a semantic perturbation pipeline to create controlled test variants.

Across 15 public benchmarks, CAFE achieves statistically significant gains over the strongest AFE baseline (Wilcoxon p<0.001, large effect) and reduces out-of-distribution performance drop by up to 4x under distribution shifts. This work shows that incorporating causal structure as a soft inductive prior can substantially improve the robustness and efficiency of automated feature engineering, addressing the brittleness of existing statistical-heuristic methods under distribution shift. It is relevant to AI/ML practitioners working with tabular data, especially in high-stakes domains where robustness to distributional changes is critical. CAFE uses hierarchical reward shaping and causal group-level exploration strategies to favor causally plausible transformations while controlling feature complexity, and it produces more compact feature sets with more stable post-hoc attributions. The approach is evaluated on both controlled covariate shifts and naturally occurring distribution shifts (Folktables), with competitive time-to-target and reduced episodes-to-convergence.

## [Confidence Scale Design Affects LLM Metacognition: 0-20 Beats 0-100](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09309) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2603.09309) shows that LLM verbalized confidence is heavily discretized, with over 78% of responses concentrating on just three round-number values on a 0-100 scale. Across six LLMs and three datasets, the authors find that a 0-20 scale consistently improves metacognitive efficiency (measured by meta-d') compared to the standard 0-100 format. This work reveals that the confidence scale itself is not a neutral design choice and can significantly affect the quality of verbalized uncertainty, which is widely used for black-box uncertainty estimation. The findings suggest that scale design should be treated as a first-class experimental variable in LLM evaluation, impacting how practitioners elicit and interpret confidence scores. The authors systematically manipulate confidence scales along granularity, boundary placement, and range regularity, and evaluate metacognitive sensitivity using meta-d'. They find that boundary compression degrades performance and round-number preferences persist even under irregular ranges, indicating a robust cognitive bias in LLM confidence reporting.

Metacognitive sensitivity, measured by meta-d', quantifies how well confidence ratings discriminate between correct and incorrect decisions, rooted in signal detection theory. AlphaCNOT introduces a reinforcement learning framework that uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to model CNOT minimization as a planning problem, achieving up to 24.62% reduction in CNOT count compared to the Patel-Markov-Hayes (PMH) baseline on linear reversible synthesis and consistent gate count reductions on various topologies with up to 8 qubits. ## [ICCU: In-Context Continual Unlearning via Pattern-Induced Refusal Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27138) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ICCU introduces an in-context continual unlearning framework that induces readable refusal rules from unlearning datasets and applies them at inference time as a filter or via the system prompt, without modifying model parameters. Because rules are accumulated as an order-independent union, ICCU is compositional and free of cross-request interference, and the original forget-set data can be discarded after rule induction. This approach addresses key challenges in continual machine unlearning, such as high cost, utility loss, and cross-request interference associated with fine-tuning-based methods. It offers a practical and compositional solution that could be highly relevant for real-world deployments where unlearning requests arrive sequentially. ICCU effectively suppresses target knowledge while preserving utility, scales across long sequences of requests, and remains robust to paraphrased, cross-lingual, and adversarially framed queries. The code is available at https://github.com/rhpan/ICCU.

## [LAGO: Hierarchical World Model Predicts Latent Subgoals from Language for Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20627) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LAGO is a hierarchical world model that uses a single predictor to both forecast action-conditioned dynamics and ground language instructions as sequences of intermediate latent subgoals, trained with a single regression objective in a shared latent space. At each planning step, it predicts latent subgoals from a language instruction and optimizes actions using a soft-minimum alignment cost, outperforming flat and hierarchical image-goal planners, especially on long-horizon navigation where it more than doubles the success rate of a goal-conditioned behavior cloning policy. This work addresses the task specification bottleneck in model-based planning by unifying language grounding and dynamics prediction in a shared latent space, avoiding noisy cross-modal alignment or dependence on separate large generative models. It could enable more flexible and efficient language-guided planning for robots and agents, particularly in long-horizon tasks with complex constraints. LAGO uses a soft-minimum alignment cost that rewards subgoal proximity without enforcing a rigid path, and it repredicts subgoals as the agent's state evolves, turning a long-horizon instruction into locally tractable objectives. Grounding language in the world model's own latent space outperforms vision-language reward models, including one that plans with ground-truth dynamics.

**Background**: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are self-supervised models that learn by predicting abstract representations of future states rather than reconstructing raw pixels, enabling planning in latent space. Model-based planning uses a learned model of the environment to simulate outcomes and select actions, but specifying tasks remains challenging: visual goals give precise local gradients but poor distant guidance, while language is flexible but suffers from noisy cross-modal alignment. Hierarchical approaches decompose long-horizon tasks into subgoals, and LAGO integrates language grounding into this framework.

## [SGPO: Strategy Distillation Outperforms Trajectory Imitation for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24064) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Strategy-Guided Policy Optimization (SGPO), which replaces instance-level trajectory imitation with reusable strategy distillation. SGPO extracts structured strategy descriptions from strong-model responses and uses a token-level forward-KL objective to selectively transfer strategic guidance into the unguided policy, with adaptive instance-level weighting to control when to distill. Experiments on four mathematical benchmarks across two model families show SGPO consistently outperforms SFT, on-policy RL, and hybrid-policy baselines, improving the average score by 2.2 points over the strongest baseline on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. This work addresses a key limitation of traditional knowledge distillation for LLM reasoning: imitating specific solution trajectories encourages memorization rather than transferable problem-solving skills. By shifting to strategy-level transfer, SGPO offers a more generalizable approach that could improve how smaller models learn to reason, impacting the broader reasoning distillation subfield. SGPO constructs both autonomous and strategy-guided trajectories for each problem to directly compare model behavior with and without strategic guidance. The forward-KL objective provides an inherently selective distillation signal that outperforms direct trajectory imitation, and strategy distillation exhibits complementary scaling with base model capability.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Knowledge distillation in LLMs often involves training a smaller student model to imitate the outputs of a larger teacher model. In reasoning tasks, this typically means imitating full solution trajectories, which can lead to rote memorization of specific steps rather than learning general reasoning strategies. Forward KL divergence is a common objective in distillation that encourages the student to match the teacher's full output distribution, but its role in reasoning distillation is nuanced. Policy optimization methods like reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) are also used to improve reasoning, but they require careful reward design.

## [CIPHER: Decoupled Exploration-Selection Framework for Test-Time Scaling of Data Science Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14386) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CIPHER introduces a Decoupled Exploration-Selection (DES) framework that scales test-time compute at the plan level by generating N candidate analysis plans, selecting M<N for parallel execution, and aggregating results. Evaluated across 48 design choices on 357 tasks from Infi-DA-Bench and InsightBench, a single zero-tuning configuration comes within 1.2pp of DataWise and 1.3pp of Agent-Poirot. This work is significant because it shows a single zero-tuning system can handle both closed-ended and open-ended data science tasks, potentially simplifying deployment of enterprise analytics agents. It also provides actionable insights on how to allocate inference budgets across generation, selection, and aggregation. The joint sweep reveals that generation and aggregation are the most influential performance levers, while random selection—the only strategy with zero overhead—matches its tuned alternatives. The study spans two base models (one proprietary, one open-weights) and 48 design choices covering generation, selection, budget, and aggregator capacity.

ArbiGraph introduces a benchmark generator that represents each task as a natural-language problem with an executable Python solver and composes tasks through typed intermediate states, enabling controllable task graphs whose length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value type can be varied while preserving exact automatic verification. Evaluating a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four topologies, it finds accuracy drops by up to 33.3% on branching chains of dependent math tasks despite high accuracy on isolated tasks. It gives agent developers a controllable, automatically verifiable benchmark for context management, a capability increasingly critical as agents tackle long-horizon, multi-step tasks. The benchmark is instantiated with math, GSM-style word-problem, and Python-tracing task categories, and its code, generated datasets, and evaluation results are released on GitHub. The design preserves exact automatic verification while varying graph topology, but the empirical evaluation covers only a single Qwen3.5-27B agent across four topologies, so broader model coverage remains to be tested.

## [xPress Adds Causal Refiner to Diffusion Drafters for Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02438) ⭐️ 7.0/10

xPress introduces a lightweight causal refiner that restores missing causality in block-diffusion drafters such as dFlash by reconciling independently sampled per-position marginals into more jointly probable sequences in a single parallel refinement pass. On Qwen3-8B across seven math, code, and chat benchmarks, it raises acceptance length by about 30% on average (up to +56%) and end-to-end decoding throughput by about 1.3× on average (up to 1.7×) compared to the original dFlash drafter. This work targets a specific inefficiency in diffusion-based speculative decoding: draft tokens sampled independently per position are individually likely but jointly improbable, causing early rejection by the target model and limiting acceptance length. By fixing this without a token-by-token loop, xPress could make block-diffusion drafters more practical for production LLM inference acceleration. The refiner operates on the whole diffusion block at once through parallel refinement, propagating causal dependencies across the draft without a sequential loop. The reported gains are measured on Qwen3-8B against the original dFlash drafter, so generalization to other target models and drafter architectures remains to be validated.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by having a small, fast draft model propose several tokens ahead, which a larger target model then verifies in parallel, accepting tokens that match its own predictions. DFlash is a speculative decoding framework that uses a lightweight block diffusion model to draft an entire block of tokens in a single forward pass, achieving up to 6× lossless acceleration on Qwen3-8B. However, the final sampling step of block diffusion draws conditionally independent tokens at each position, producing per-position marginals rather than a joint distribution, which can yield sequences that are individually plausible but jointly unlikely under the target model.

## [LLM Refusal Shows Broken Symmetry: Answer Release Is Local, Refusal Restoration Is Not](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15772) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Using matched answering and refusal trajectories with bidirectional activation patching, the authors demonstrate a causal asymmetry in LLM refusal: the correct answer remains linearly recoverable from hidden states even during a clean refusal, and releasing it requires only a single-position patch, whereas reimposing suppression demands broader multi-position interventions. They term this phenomenon 'broken symmetry' and show that an average answer-to-refusal displacement vector fails as a reliable reversible linear control toggle. This finding challenges the assumption that refusal is a simple symmetric switch and has direct implications for AI safety and auditing: probe recoverability can overestimate true behavioral control, and locating refusal-relevant directions does not reliably grant the ability to steer a model from answering to coherent refusal. It suggests that safety mechanisms based on linear probes or steering vectors may be less robust than previously thought. The study uses a controlled withhold setting to obtain perfectly matched answering and refusal trajectories, enabling clean bidirectional activation patching. The asymmetry is causal: releasing a withheld answer is highly local (single-position patch), while assembling a coherent refusal sequence is more difficult and requires distributed interventions, and the average displacement vector between states does not act as a reversible toggle.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a key technique in mechanistic interpretability: it runs a model on two inputs (one where a behavior appears, one where it doesn't) and systematically replaces activations from one run with those from the other to localize causal components. Linear probing of hidden states is commonly used to detect whether information (such as a withheld answer) is present, but presence does not guarantee behavioral control. This paper connects these methods to study whether refusal is a localized suppression or a distributed process.

SAPO proposes a single-rollout PPO-style framework that unifies policy optimization and value learning within a single causal LLM by generating action and value estimates at distinct causal boundaries with shared parameters, and jointly optimizing PPO objectives with an auxiliary on-policy SARSA objective using turn-level generalized advantage estimation. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-14B show a 24.8% reduction in peak GPU memory and 23.1% reduction in per-iteration runtime versus a strong PPO baseline, while matching or slightly improving task success rate and outperforming GRPO and recent variants in success and training stability. By unifying policy and value learning in one model with a single rollout, SAPO offers a more resource-efficient path to stable agentic RL, which could lower the cost of post-training LLM agents for practitioners. SAPO exploits the autoregressive structure of LLMs to sequentially produce action and value estimation at distinct causal boundaries with shared parameters, and adds an auxiliary on-policy SARSA objective with turn-level generalized advantage estimation to facilitate value learning. The reported gains are measured against a strong PPO baseline on ALFWorld and WebShop, and the method is also shown to outperform GRPO and recent cutting-edge variants in both task success and training stability.

## [Counterfactual Latent World Models Fix 'Counterfactual Collapse' in Embodied AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05834) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper identifies a failure mode called 'counterfactual collapse' in pretrained world models, where models predict visually plausible futures but fail to distinguish interventions with different behavioral consequences. It introduces Counterfactual Latent World Models (CLWM), combining a recurrent belief-state encoder, action-conditioned latent dynamics, and a contrastive counterfactual objective, improving planning success from 65.1% to 74.6% on Occluded Push and from 67.3% to 78.9% on Aliased Maze. This work highlights that prediction quality alone is insufficient for actionable world models, which is critical as embodied AI increasingly relies on large-scale pretrained representations. The proposed counterfactual separability metric can audit any encoder before a planner trusts it, potentially improving safety and reliability in robotics and autonomous systems. CLWM reduces exploitative planning failures from 18.4% to 9.7% on Deferred Kitchen, with ablations showing gains come from hard counterfactual negatives, especially perceptual-alias negatives. The counterfactual separability metric correlates with planning success across five baseline model classes (r ≥ 0.94) but has not yet been measured on large-scale pretrained encoders.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: World models learn predictive dynamics of an environment so agents can plan and act without direct interaction. In partially observable settings, agents must maintain belief states—distributions over hidden states—to act optimally. Pretrained encoders are typically optimized for perceptual similarity, which can discard intervention-relevant information, leading to counterfactual collapse. Counterfactual reasoning involves imagining outcomes of alternative actions, essential for robust decision-making.

## [LLM In-Context Learning in Multi-Agent Games Relies on Statistical Extrapolation, Not Recursive Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18591) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.18591v2) shows that when the statistical patterns in historical feedback are disrupted, the benefits of longer context for LLM agents in multi-agent incomplete-information games largely vanish, degrading decision quality to the no-context baseline. This effect is sharply amplified by stronger strategic interdependence, suggesting that in-context learning (ICL) in such settings is better explained by statistical extrapolation than by recursive belief reasoning. This finding challenges the assumption that LLM agents engage in genuine strategic reasoning in multi-agent settings, which is critical for applications like negotiation, market simulation, and cooperative AI. It also introduces a reusable diagnostic framework that could reshape how researchers evaluate LLM reasoning capabilities. The study uses a public goods game with manipulated statistical structure of historical feedback and benchmarks decision quality against a history-independent rational expectations equilibrium (REE). The degradation to no-context baseline is amplified by stronger strategic interdependence, and the authors propose REE as a diagnostic tool for distinguishing reasoning from extrapolation.

**Background**: In-context learning (ICL) allows LLMs to improve task performance by conditioning on examples or interaction history in the prompt without updating model weights. Recursive belief reasoning is the cognitive ability to model others' beliefs about one's own beliefs, essential for strategic interactions in multi-agent games. A rational expectations equilibrium (REE) is an economic benchmark where agents' beliefs coincide with the actual law of motion of the economy, providing a history-independent optimal decision baseline.

Forecast-Dojo introduces a replayable environment that reconstructs 1,568 resolved Polymarket events into dated forecasting steps, paired with 18.8 million dated news articles, to enable reproducible evaluation and training of LLM forecasting agents. Across 12 models, research tools consistently improved forecasting, yet all models still trailed historical market forecasts, and fine-tuning Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 on trajectories from Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 raised accuracy from 34.8% to 42.8%. The environment splits events temporally into training and evaluation sets, and findings show that greater capture of new evidence correlates with larger improvements over time, while carrying a belief notebook across dates reduces research costs without consistently improving forecast quality. ## [Skill Cascading Attacks: Distributed Malice Across Modular Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30383) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces skill cascading attacks, a threat paradigm in which a malicious objective is split across multiple modular skills so each skill appears benign in isolation but their combined execution causes harm. The authors release SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework, and SkillCascade-Bench, a benchmark of 213 validated cascading test cases across multiple agent systems and domains. The work exposes a gap between component-level integrity and system-level safety, showing that existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors can be evaded when malicious intent is distributed across skills. This matters for anyone deploying third-party skill ecosystems in LLM agents, since it calls for defenses that reason over cross-skill interactions rather than inspecting skills in isolation. The paper illustrates the attack with a prescription-review pipeline where one skill weakens signals of recently discontinued medications, a second downgrades the severity of drug interactions tied to them, and a third suppresses the resulting low-priority alert, silently removing a severe warning before it reaches the physician. Cascaded interactions reliably induced harmful behavior across representative agents such as OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex, as well as multiple LLM backbones.

## [DISCERN benchmark tests AI agents across full scientific research workflow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33357) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced DISCERN (Data Integrity and Scientific Capability: Evidence, Reasoning, and Novelty), a controlled benchmark on real public datasets that evaluates AI agents at three levels: data integrity, analysis verification under confounds and tool traps, and hypothesis generation and revision under adversarial review. Across 203 tasks in eight life-science tracks and eight models, agents achieved perfect scores in only 60.8% of Level 1, 34.2% of Level 2, and 0.6% of Level 3 evaluations. Existing benchmarks typically test analytical task completion or hypothesis generation in isolation, so DISCERN fills a gap by evaluating whether reliable evidence supports valid and novel claims across the entire automated research pipeline. Its findings suggest that strong aggregate performance can mask level-specific weaknesses, indicating that current agents are not yet ready for reliable autonomous scientific analysis or discovery. The benchmark includes counterfactual cases where evidence consistent with real data and documented phenomena conflicts with established expectations, forcing agents to propose alternative explanations and testable hypotheses. Penalties were attributed to rejection of sound data, failure to carry recognized limitations into conclusions, and wide variation in hypothesis production, while cross-track rankings by token and code use were more stable than rankings by evidence judgment.

## [EOPSA fixes supervisory collapse and gradient dilution in on-policy self-distilled safety alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34519) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper diagnoses two bottlenecks in On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) for safety alignment: supervisory collapse over extended rollouts, where the teacher's corrective signal degrades as the student's prefix lengthens, and gradient dilution from stylistic shifts, where safety-irrelevant stylistic differences dominate the distillation objective. It proposes EOPSA, which combines Adaptive Rollout Scheduling guided by a Teacher Rescue Rate (TRR) metric with Selective Distillation that filters out safety-neutral tokens, and reports ~50% reduction in rollout computation and backpropagation through only ~2% of tokens while outperforming full-token distillation baselines on models up to 32B parameters. Safety alignment methods often impose a 'safety tax' that degrades general reasoning, and OPSD's inefficiencies make that trade-off worse; EOPSA shows that concentrating supervision on reliably supervised, safety-critical tokens can cut training cost substantially while preserving reasoning. This is directly relevant to researchers and practitioners aligning large reasoning models, where rollout and backprop costs are major barriers. EOPSA's two mechanisms are coordinated: Adaptive Rollout Scheduling dynamically bounds the generation horizon using the novel Teacher Rescue Rate metric to stay within reliable supervision regimes, while Selective Distillation restricts gradient updates to safety-pivotal transitions. Evaluations cover reasoning models up to 32B parameters, but the approach is a specialized refinement of OPSD rather than a new paradigm, and its benefits depend on the quality of the privileged teacher prompts.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) aligns a language model by having it generate its own rollouts and then distilling token-level supervision from a frozen teacher copy of the same model conditioned on privileged prompts, such as refusal-oriented instructions. This provides dense per-token feedback at lower sampling cost than reinforcement learning methods like GRPO, but prior work has noted that on-policy distillation can collapse into long repetitive outputs and that privileged prompting can introduce stylistic artifacts. EOPSA builds on this line by identifying where the teacher's supervision becomes unreliable and where gradients are wasted on style rather than safety.

The framework is grounded in an opportunity-loss decomposition of expected terminal improvement and achieves an average Max-score rank of 1.72 across 14 configurations on 32 benchmark groups, securing top score in 23 groups. ## [Stacked LLM and rule gates for agents fail dependently, study finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07359) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07359v2) empirically tests whether stacked runtime gates for agent tool calls fail independently, using 1,119 labelled agent actions from three corpora. It finds that any two LLM judges compose to only about 1.2–1.4 multiplication-equivalent layers (n_mult) under the STRICT miss definition, while a deterministic rule layer plus one judge composes to 1.86–2.09 layers, far below the assumed multiplication of errors. This challenges the common assumption that stacking multiple runtime gates multiplicatively reduces failure rates, which underpins many AI safety architectures for LLM agents. If gates fail dependently, adding more LLM judges yields diminishing returns, affecting how practitioners design guardrails for agent tool calls. The study reports phi coefficients (median +0.430 for judge pairs, 6 of 6 significant; median +0.014 for rule+judge, 0 of 4 significant) and notes that solo accuracy does not predict added joint coverage—a cloud rule pack cut the rule layer's solo miss rate by 20% but added no new joint coverage. It also documents an unrequested model version serving one judge tier in 50 of 112 batches, which overturned a pre-declared analysis rule and reversed five conclusions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Runtime gates are checks placed before or after an LLM agent's tool calls to block unsafe actions, and they can be deterministic rules or LLM-based judges. The multiplication-of-errors assumption holds that if each gate has an independent miss probability, stacking N gates reduces the overall miss rate to the product of individual rates. The phi coefficient measures correlation between binary outcomes, so a high phi between two gates indicates their failures are dependent rather than independent.

## [MedEvo: Knowledge-guided trajectory repair boosts medical multimodal reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17690) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MedEvo introduces a method that uses a medical tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis to repair failed reasoning trajectories and select training data, improving Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone. It also raises Qwen3.5-35B and Qwen3.5-397B mean accuracy from 67.91% to 73.04% and from 71.83% to 74.95%, respectively, surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). MedEvo uses a gold-blind auditor to locate the first consequential error and provide a minimal, answer-free hint, allowing the same student to retain the valid prefix and regenerate the erroneous suffix; after each round, it identifies capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set to prioritize related questions. Analyses show that repair success does not imply learning value and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.

A new arXiv study found that three experienced loan underwriters and processors, recruited via Upwork, identified only 14 edit-supported concerns (10.6%) out of 132 file-level judgements when reviewing AI-edited financial documents in a first-pass, document-only setting. All supported concerns involved identifier inconsistencies within or across documents, and no reported visual cue correctly identified an actual edit. The findings suggest that human review alone is insufficient for catching AI-assisted document forgery, which has direct implications for fraud detection in lending and underwriting workflows. They motivate supplementing human reviewers with automated consistency checks and independent source verification to reduce fraud risk. The study used 134 forged PDFs derived from 47 genuine financial documents, with edits preserving amounts, dates, and balances but introducing identifier inconsistencies that were knowingly retained. Limitations include a small sample of three reviewer-package pairs and no genuine-file controls, so the results describe an exploratory setting rather than population-wide detection accuracy.

## [Decision-Theoretic Framework Values Memory in Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31303) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The arXiv paper 2610.31303v2 proposes a decision-theoretic framework that traces the value of memory in language agents from raw history through persistent state, operational use, and costly recovery and revision. It expresses original and retained value in units of avoided task loss, introduces risk-cost frontiers, and uses five minimal counterexamples to expose the roles of information timing, retrieval access, component interaction, feedback, and demand uncertainty. This work offers a principled way to reason about when memory is worth preserving, using, or revising, which could inform the design of more reliable and cost-effective memory systems for LLM-based agents. It connects abstract memory distinctions to operational risk bounds and testable principles, potentially influencing how agent memory is evaluated and allocated in practice. The framework includes a cost-aware simulation condition and diagnostics on LoCoMo, a two-project update task, and longitudinal cases that reveal failures of preservation, use, and measurement. Notably, it shows that a pointer with zero mutual information about the answer can still reduce the cost of exact recovery, and that at fixed retrieved evidence, a saved ledger changes subsequent answers, while at fixed agent outputs, an evaluator revision changes scores.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 27, 04:00

**Background**: Language agents are AI systems that use large language models to make decisions and take actions over multiple steps, often relying on memory to retain information from past interactions. Memory in such agents can be stored as raw history, compressed state, or pointers, but its value depends on whether the agent can actually use the retained information when needed. Decision theory provides a formal way to evaluate choices under uncertainty, and this paper applies it to quantify memory's worth in terms of avoided task loss.

The paper introduces Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD to address global rank allocation and decomposition quality in SVD-based LLM compression. LEMS uses a layer-wise error surrogate with local/global importance and propagation bias, solved via ILP, while KFAC-SVD uses token-wise statistics to mitigate rank collapse. This work delivers up to 4.7 percentage point zero-shot accuracy gains and 19% average perplexity improvement over existing methods, validated on Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 up to 70B parameters. It advances low-rank compression as a practical way to reduce LLM inference costs without retraining. LEMS formulates global rank allocation as an Integer Linear Program (ILP) using a calibrated error surrogate, while KFAC-SVD replaces Fisher-based estimators with token-wise statistics to avoid rank deficiency. The methods are evaluated across multiple model families and generalize to 70B-scale models.

Researchers introduce COAT (Causal representatiOn AssistanT), a framework that uses large language models to propose measured variables from unstructured data for causal discovery. COAT iteratively refines these proposals using feedback from causal discovery results, with variants COAT-MB for Markov Blanket discovery and COAT-PAG for learning partial ancestral graphs. This work addresses a longstanding bottleneck in causal discovery: the reliance on human experts to define high-quality variables. By automating variable proposal with LLMs, it could broaden the application of causal discovery to unstructured data like text and images, impacting fields from epidemiology to social science. COAT does not directly infer causality with LLMs; instead, it uses LLM-proposed variables as inputs to traditional causal discovery algorithms and feeds back results to refine proposals. ## [LLM-designed decoy nudges show mixed cross-country results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12045) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A preregistered field experiment with 3,495 participants across five countries found that decoy parameters identified by large language models (LLMs) as optimal for a given country produced stronger nudging effects than non-optimal parameters in the United States and marginally in Germany, but not in China, India, or Singapore. However, there was no evidence that LLM-informed personalized decoys outperformed country-level optimal decoys. This study provides a rigorous test of using LLMs to design personalized nudges, showing that while LLMs can help identify effective country-level decoy parameters, personalization may not yield additional benefits. The null findings on personalization and cross-country variation are valuable for understanding the limits of LLM-driven behavioral interventions. The experiment was preregistered and involved 3,495 participants in five countries. The authors also demonstrated that LLM-generated data can serve as informative priors for Bayesian choice models, improving predictive performance and parameter estimation with smaller human samples, yielding estimated reductions of 37-75% in human sample size at matched predictive performance.

ParallaxRAG enforces relational diversity across multiple heads while constraining weakly related paths, constructing cleaner subgraphs and guiding LLMs through grounded, hop-wise reasoning. RECAP dynamically reweights training objectives based on online signals of convergence and instability, shifting focus from saturated objectives to underperforming or volatile ones; it is end-to-end and compatible with existing RLVR pipelines. The graph-aware curriculum uses an easy-to-hard biased sampler to improve RL for moderate-sized LLMs, and trajectory analyses show GraphDancer retrieves answer-bearing evidence more often, achieves higher accuracy when such evidence is found, and substantially reduces invalid-protocol outcomes. Stability of DAG follows from a weak contraction property, and analysis inside real cross-attention layers shows that the alignment between the discrepancy and the retrieval direction is observed throughout sampling. The method adds only a small cost per image over the base sampler, though it is an incremental guidance-method advance rather than a paradigm shift.

## [LinearARD: Linear-Memory Attention Distillation for RoPE Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00004) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LinearARD introduces an attention-structure distillation method that restores RoPE-scaled LLMs by aligning row-wise distributions of Q/Q, K/K, and V/V self-relation matrices from the final attention layer with a frozen native-RoPE teacher. It uses a linear-activation-memory kernel that stores only per-token log-sum-exp statistics and recomputes logits in the backward pass to avoid quadratic memory costs. This method drastically reduces the data and compute needed for context extension, recovering over 93% of native short-context performance using only 4.25M tokens—about 1.6% of the 256M-token budget required by state-of-the-art baselines. It offers a more efficient alternative to continued pre-training for long-context LLMs. Across LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA3-8B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1 extended to 32K context, LinearARD achieves 93.1%/94.2%/94.3% recovery of native short-context performance and strong long-context robustness on RULER. Under the same constrained budget, CPT and LongReD remain near zero on RULER, highlighting the efficiency-quality tradeoff.

## [Numeral Base and Tokenization Shape Grokking Delay in Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13082) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2604.13082v3) studies one-step Collatz prediction with transformers and finds that grokking (delayed generalization) occurs mainly when the training set contains few distinct integers, and that the numeral base determines how many integers are needed. Bases where each output digit depends on only a few neighboring input digits require several times fewer training examples. This work shows that the choice of numeral representation can predict sample efficiency before training, offering a principled way to improve arithmetic performance in LLMs by designing better tokenization schemes. It also cautions that high linear-probe accuracy does not reliably indicate that a model has learned to compute the probed features. The authors predicted the ordering of bases by carry structure before training, and confirmed it holds for a second Collatz map, integer division, a decoder-only transformer, and across three model sizes; input length does not explain the effect. A linear probe recovers low-order residues equally well from randomly initialized and trained encoders, undermining probe-based claims of learned computation.

**Background**: Grokking, or delayed generalization, is a phenomenon where a neural network first memorizes the training data and only much later generalizes to unseen data. The Collatz conjecture defines a sequence where each term is half the previous if even, or three times plus one if odd, and is a classic testbed for arithmetic reasoning. Tokenization, the process of splitting numbers or text into tokens, is known to affect how well language models handle arithmetic.

## [Residual Connections and Symmetry Breaking Explain Geometric Continuity in Deep Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04971) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.04971v2) identifies residual connections and symmetry-breaking nonlinearities as the two mechanisms that produce geometric continuity—where principal singular vectors of adjacent weight matrices point in similar directions—in deep networks. Through toy MLP and small transformer experiments, the authors show that a rotation-equivariant nonlinearity achieves less than half of ReLU's continuity, isolating symmetry breaking as the key ingredient. This work provides a theoretical explanation for a widely observed but previously unexplained phenomenon in deep learning, potentially informing model compression and architecture design. It also clarifies the distinct roles of activation functions and normalization layers in shaping weight structure. The study finds that activation functions concentrate continuity in the leading singular direction, while normalization distributes it across multiple directions. In transformers, continuity is projection-specific: Q, K, Gate, and Up develop input-space continuity, O and Down develop output-space continuity, and V alone lacks high continuity due to the absence of an adjacent nonlinearity.

## [Neural Information Causality: A Capacity Law for Learned Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09316) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces 'Neural Information Causality' (Neural-IC), a representation law stating that the aggregate information recoverable from a learned representation across later queries cannot exceed the physically specified interface capacity, even with pre-established quantum resources. It provides a decomposition separating capacity slack, jointly organized information, and answer-production losses, and shows in a nested Bell-correlation construction that quantum assistance improves average retrieval over the optimal classical one-bit benchmark. This work bridges machine learning theory and physics by linking representation learning to information causality and physical interface capacity, offering a design principle for memory allocation, encoding objectives, and decoder outputs. It could influence how practitioners think about the limits of learned representations and the role of quantum resources in retrieval tasks. The law is derived for a fresh database of independent bits, and exhaustive evaluation of trained binary codes reveals why nearly full use of a memory's information budget can coexist with limited retrieval. The quantum advantage is demonstrated only in a specific nested Bell-correlation construction, not as a general result.

## [Mixture-Density Model Eliminates Flying Points in Depth Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02552) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose MDA, a mixture-density representation that predicts multiple depth hypotheses and their probabilities per pixel, eliminating flying-point artifacts at object boundaries. Across different architectures, MDA substantially improves boundary reconstruction and removes flying points even under severe input blur, with negligible runtime overhead. Flying points are a persistent failure mode that contaminates 3D geometry at object boundaries, affecting downstream tasks like 3D reconstruction and autonomous navigation. This approach addresses the root cause—single-depth modeling—and naturally extends to transparent objects and sky regions, potentially improving depth estimation in real-world scenes. MDA lets the model predict multiple depth hypotheses per pixel and selects the decoded depth from one hypothesis rather than an intermediate value, avoiding empty-space placements. The framework also handles transparent objects by predicting multiple depth layers and separates unbounded sky from finite-depth regions, producing flying-point-free skylines.

Flying points are spurious 3D points that appear in empty space between foreground and background surfaces, typically at object boundaries where a pixel straddles two surfaces. Standard models assign a single depth per pixel, which forces an intermediate depth that lies on neither surface, causing these artifacts. Mixture density networks, which output a probability distribution over multiple values, offer a way to represent such ambiguity.

A new arXiv paper (2606.19111v2) operationalizes three classical leadership styles—transactional, transformational, and situational—as controllers over a shared action vocabulary (explore, revise, accept, synthesize) in multi-agent LLM teams. This work bridges team science and multi-agent LLM coordination, showing that process-level leadership often adds little accuracy and that arbitrary-rule controllers fail to recover, which sets important boundary conditions for designing LLM team coordination mechanisms. It suggests that accuracy alone is insufficient to evaluate coordination control and that behavioral signatures like recovery from incorrect consensus are crucial. The study uses behavioral signatures (majority lock-in, exploration, recovery from an incorrect round-0 consensus) and per-action ablations, finding that a matched controller with the same actions but an arbitrary rule recovers no better than majority voting. A recovery-advantage account tested with four boundary probes posits that a controller beats plain interaction only where the round-0 majority is unreliable, the task is recoverable, and undirected interaction does not already repair it; the positive side is observed in only one combination (llama-4-scout social), so the readiness-gap boundary is advanced as an explanatory hypothesis, not an established principle.

It also highlights a fundamental limitation of relying solely on AUROC for encoder selection in medical imaging. CANDOR defines a positive image as discordant when its k nearest negatives are on average more similar to it than its k nearest positives; the discordance rate D has a chance level of 1/2 with equal-sized candidate sets. On chest test splits, linear heads missed 0.301 of discordant positives versus 0.165 of other positives, and computing D requires only one forward pass per image.

## [Abstention Options in Bias Benchmarks Distort Fairness Scores of Distilled Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28639) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2607.28639v3) identifies three mechanisms—refusal loss, sampling churn, and option capture—that cause abstention options in multiple-choice bias benchmarks to misrepresent the fairness of distilled small language models. The authors show that aggregate scores only capture outright refusal loss, while per-item scores are confounded by sampling churn and remapping, and that conditioning on committed answers is necessary to avoid misreading moved refusal mass as fairness. This work matters because distilled small language models are increasingly deployed on phones, cars, and offline assistants, and their fairness is often judged by multiple-choice bias scores that include an abstention option. The paper demonstrates that common metrics can report improvements whenever refusal mass moves, even when the model becomes less fair, which could lead to unsafe deployment decisions. Resampling a reference model across inference seeds already turns 10% to 27% of its refusals into stereotype answers, so a per-item refusal metric reported without that floor overstates damage. Option capture is particularly severe: students trained with refusal exemplars take an offered abstention option on up to 95% of science questions where abstention is never correct, and the habit carries to three further benchmarks.

## [CallScreenBench benchmarks small on-device models as phone secretaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01033) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CallScreenBench is a new benchmark (arXiv:2608.01033) that evaluates small, 4-bit quantized language models (0.6–4B parameters across three model families) acting as phone secretaries that answer unknown, potentially adversarial inbound calls without an oracle. It reports five automated call-and-note measure groups motivated by whether the owner would endorse how their proxy handled the call, plus three guardedness diagnostics, and deliberately defines no benchmark-wide composite or leaderboard score. Most agent benchmarks assume a cooperative user with a well-defined task, so this work reframes evaluation around delegated, adversarial interaction where the caller holds the goal — a setting that matters as quantized SLMs make on-device automation plausible. Its finding that bare scam-side detection rewards universal suspicion, and that rankings shift when legitimate-call false positives are counted, is a caution for anyone building or auditing on-device call-screening agents. The benchmark covers only the text-domain conversational decision layer, explicitly excluding speech recognition, audio interaction, end-to-end latency, and actual handset execution. Each measure is paired where possible with a counter-metric and uncertainty estimate, and scripted degenerate agents expose floors — for example, a hangup-and-echo policy achieves entity recall of 1.000 — while triage discrimination orders the model checkpoints differently from the service, recall, and plausibility measures.

## [LC-GRPO bridges train-inference gap in flow-based GRPO with Langevin correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05600) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces LC-GRPO, a flow-based GRPO framework that replaces standard SDE rollouts with an inference-aligned ODE Euler step followed by a Langevin correction targeting the marginal at each timestep. The required score is recovered directly from the flow velocity without an extra score model, keeping transitions as isotropic Gaussians with tractable likelihood. This addresses a real and underexplored mismatch between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic ODE inference in RL fine-tuning of flow-based generative models, which can degrade sample quality as exploration noise grows. The method could improve reward optimization for text-to-image and text-to-video models without sacrificing generation fidelity. The authors theoretically show that under suitable conditions a single Langevin correction step reduces the error of an imperfect ODE Euler step and, under matched randomness, yields a more accurate transition than Euler–Maruyama discretization of the reverse SDE. Experiments on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo show consistent reward improvement and preserved generation quality.

**Background**: Flow-based generative models sample by solving a deterministic ODE that transports noise to data, while reinforcement learning typically requires stochastic rollouts for exploration. Existing online RL methods for flow models therefore swap the inference-time ODE for an SDE during training, but finite-step discretization can make SDE rollouts blurry and misaligned with ODE inference. GRPO is a value-network-free RL algorithm that estimates baselines from groups of sampled answers, and Langevin correction is a score-based sampling technique that adds noise and follows the score to improve sample quality.

## [LoRAScan Detects Backdoor Triggers in LoRA Adapters via Down-Projection Activation Spikes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06795) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LoRAScan is introduced as the first adapter-aware defense that detects and rejects trigger-bearing inputs at inference time without modifying adapter parameters. It identifies a small subset of LoRA insertion sites (about 5%) that remain stable on clean inputs but show concentrated spikes in down-projection activations when a trigger is present, rejecting 98.49% of malicious inputs with a low error rate on clean inputs. This addresses a real supply-chain security gap: untrusted LoRA adapters can inject backdoors that cause harmful outputs, and existing adapter-agnostic defenses dilute the signal while adapter-aware methods only flag entire adapters. By enabling safe use of potentially compromised adapters at inference time, LoRAScan could improve security for practitioners distributing and deploying LoRA adapters in LLM ecosystems. LoRAScan pre-identifies low-variance insertion sites before deployment and monitors them during inference, focusing on down-projection activations where trigger-induced spikes are highly concentrated. It outperforms existing defenses across standard LLM backdoor benchmarks, though the abstract does not detail the error rate on clean inputs or the computational overhead of monitoring.

## [Defense-as-Skill: Runtime Guard Evolved as Installable Skill for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01487) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Defense-as-Skill, a paradigm in which the runtime guard (SkillSonar) is itself an installable, inspectable, and editable skill that checks untrusted task skills' sensitive actions against the user's task boundary, routing each action to allow, replan, or confirmation without modifying the agent runtime. It also introduces SCOPE-R, a task-conditioned dataset with 6 risk families, 21 sub-categories, 206 attack-confirmed malicious instances, and 43 benign tasks, and uses Monte-Carlo Tree Search to evolve the guard skill, reducing in-distribution attack success rate from 0.482 to 0.104 and out-of-distribution ASR from 0.606 to 0.115 on repeated GLM-5 runs. Skill-augmented agents give malicious skills a durable channel to steer future actions, so pre-install vetting is insufficient and runtime, task-conditioned protection becomes necessary. Making the guard itself a transparent, evolvable skill artifact could make agent security more inspectable and adaptable across models and risk families, affecting developers deploying skills in agents like Claude Code and OpenClaw. SkillSonar operates alongside untrusted task skills and makes allow, replan, or confirmation decisions without altering the underlying agent runtime, and its evolution via Monte-Carlo Tree Search uses feedback from rollouts on the SCOPE-R training subset. Gains are reported to transfer across victim models, held-out risk families, and external benchmarks, though the abstract provides limited detail and the work is an arXiv preprint.

A new arXiv paper (2609.31107v2) pulls back the Fisher information metric through the surrogate posterior map to derive a local sensitivity tensor, yielding an upper bound on gradients of reparameterizable acquisition functions in Bayesian optimization. The gradient bound applies specifically to reparameterizable acquisition functions, which is a notable scope limitation.

**Background**: Bayesian optimization is a sequential model-based strategy for globally optimizing expensive black-box functions, using a surrogate model (often a Gaussian process) and an acquisition function to decide where to sample next. This paper connects these ideas by treating the surrogate posterior as a statistical manifold and pulling back its Fisher metric to the input space.

## [IG-VLA internalizes future imagination into a compact token for efficient robotic manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02626) ⭐️ 7.0/10

IG-VLA introduces a vision-language-action framework with Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning that imagines task-relevant future scene evolution in visual representation space, and a Scene Gist Memory that compresses reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate, and the gist policy achieves up to 6.38x speedup, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. This work addresses a key bottleneck in embodied AI: adding explicit future reasoning to VLA models is powerful but computationally expensive, and IG-VLA shows that the benefits can be retained at inference time without pixel-level video generation. The large latency reduction makes future-aware reasoning more practical for real-time robotic deployment, potentially influencing how VLA systems are designed for efficiency. The approach avoids costly pixel-level video generation by performing imagination directly in latent visual representation space, and the Scene Gist Token captures general scene context and action patterns rather than the full future reasoning trajectory. Experiments are conducted on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench, with the reported speedup measured per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU.

## [PIT-GCL: Topological Graph Contrastive Learning for Protein Binding Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04850) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PIT-GCL is a dual-tower structure-aware framework that predicts protein binding by combining ESM-2 sequence embeddings with persistent homology descriptors from Cα point clouds, without requiring bound complex structures. It outperforms sequence-based, structure-aware, and task-specific baselines on general PPI (PPIRef) and is the only method above chance on PPB-Affinity, though it is outranked by a task-specific sequence model on TCR-pMHC. This work addresses a key gap in computational biology: structure-aware binding prediction at screening scale, where bound complex structures are unavailable. By enabling precomputation of per-protein representations, it offers a practical route for large-scale therapeutic binder design and target identification. Each protein tower fuses residue-level ESM-2 embeddings with topological summaries from H0 and H1 persistence landscapes of a Vietoris-Rips filtration, processed by a structure-aware Transformer with learned attention bias from pairwise Cα distances. A bidirectional cross-attention module performs latent soft docking, and training combines binary cross-entropy with an NT-Xent contrastive objective.

Persistent homology is a topological data analysis technique that captures multiscale shape features of point clouds, and the Vietoris-Rips filtration is a common way to compute it. ESM-2 is a protein language model that provides rich sequence embeddings.

## [Greedy Local Learning for LM Pretraining: Loss Gaps and Objective Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04867) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A token-budget-matched empirical study at 125M and 400M parameters with K∈{1,2,4} blocks measures how greedy block-wise local learning's loss gap behaves in autoregressive LM pretraining. It finds that the gap more than doubles from K=2 to K=4 but shrinks from 125M to 400M at K=4, and that a Transformer-based auxiliary recovers 22-41% of the gap. Local learning removes the backward pass between blocks, making inter-stage communication forward-only and enabling independent optimizer steps—properties directly relevant to decentralized model-parallel training. Understanding how the loss gap scales and which auxiliary designs reduce it is essential for deciding whether local learning can be a viable alternative to end-to-end backpropagation for large language models. Replacing an MLP auxiliary with a Transformer-based one is a strong network-side intervention, while a multi-token-prediction (MTP) auxiliary helps only at the first block boundary and hurts at deeper boundaries; restricting MTP to the first block yields the best K=4 configuration (+0.062 vs. +0.075 nats at 400M). Deployment-style per-block execution also reduces activation memory by up to 2.2×.

**Background**: Greedy block-wise local learning splits a neural network into gradient-isolated blocks, each trained with its own local auxiliary loss, which eliminates the backward pass between blocks and allows forward-only communication. This is attractive for decentralized model-parallel training, but prior work showed it trades a worse best loss for parallel speedup on small Transformers. The Chinchilla-optimal token budget refers to the compute-optimal allocation of model size and training tokens (roughly 20 tokens per parameter) established by Hoffmann et al.

## [Harness Search Gains May Be Illusory, Preregistered Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05533) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A preregistered study with models from 1.7B to 14B parameters reports all 65 primary endpoints and finds that turning thinking off raised accuracy over a capped thinking setting in 7 of 12 model-benchmark cells, mostly because the capped setting left questions without a readable answer. For small models, the thinking-off setting was not meaningfully worse than a rescue configuration in 7 of 9 cells, and at 14B two GEPA-selected harnesses beat it by 30 to 34 points on LongevityBench letter tasks but were not detectably above the strongest constant-label baseline. The findings suggest that many reported gains from harness search—optimizing prompts, token budgets, or parsers around a frozen model—may stem from evaluation defects, unreadable answers, or weak baselines rather than genuine model improvement. This has direct implications for researchers and practitioners who rely on such optimization to claim progress, urging more rigorous evaluation and baseline reporting. From a start capped at 64 tokens, GEPA repaired the 1.7B model's harness, but at 14B no proposal of either search scored above zero; replication through the same pipeline reproduced a defect's distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases, 7 of which are fixed by an identity of the design. Descriptively, longevity fine-tuning raised a 1.7B model's letter accuracy by 41 points while cutting MMLU-Pro and GSM8K accuracy by 16 and 63 points, and on a second GPU 58% of its zero-temperature token sequences changed.

## [SNAP: Fixing Synthetic Hard Negatives in Vision-Language Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09700) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper analyzes six representation-space synthesis strategies for hard negatives in vision-language pretraining, identifies two failure modes (cross-modal negatives that are too easy or pulled toward the query, and intra-modal negatives that include the matched positive), and observes logit-scale saturation with learnable temperature. The authors propose SNAP, a model-agnostic method that generates intra-modal hard negatives never involving the positive from either modality, and show consistent gains on CLIP and FLIP across zero-shot retrieval, zero-shot classification, and linear probing. Hard negatives are known to strengthen contrastive learning, but naively transferring representation-space synthesis from unimodal self-supervised learning to vision-language pretraining can backfire. This work provides a geometric diagnosis of why such transfers fail and offers a simple, low-overhead fix that could improve a wide range of multimodal models without external generative models. SNAP adds less than 10% training time overhead, requires no external generative models, and is evaluated on top of CLIP and FLIP across multiple architectures and datasets. The paper also finds that fixing the temperature, rather than learning it, improves downstream performance when training with synthetic hard negatives due to logit-scale saturation.

The paper introduces Combinatorial Data Selection (CDS), a framework that separates sample attribution from subset selection and explicitly models non-additive interactions among training samples. It proposes Mixture-then-Select, a two-stage algorithm that first allocates sample counts per domain and then ranks samples within each domain, outperforming strong baselines by 20–54% on a real instruction-tuning data pool. The framework also extends to budget-constrained data purchasing, making it relevant to both researchers and practitioners curating instruction-tuning datasets. The theoretical guarantee states that the gap to the optimal subset is linear in the selection size and independent of the data pool size, and the method is reported to be robust across different attribution methods, models, and data pool sizes. The work is an arXiv preprint (v2) and has not yet undergone peer review.
